stories.Headline: Appeals court lifts block on Mississippi's DEI ban, ejects judge over AI errors
stories.Summary:
A federal appeals court on Thursday revived Mississippi's ban on diversity, equity and inclusion programs in public schools, wiping out a lower-court order that had kept the law from taking effect. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit, based in New Orleans, ruled that the preliminary injunction issued by U.S. District Judge Henry Wingate could not stand. The three-judge panel also reassigned the lawsuit to a different district judge after finding that the original ruling was marred by errors tied to artificial intelligence. The case is Jackson Federation of Teachers et al. v. Lynn Fitch et al., number 25-60496.

The appeals court recognized the state's authority over curricula and said the law does not directly regulate students' speech. The law at issue is House Bill 1193, which the Mississippi Legislature enacted in 2025. It bars public schools and public postsecondary institutions from creating, promoting or implementing DEI programs, from maintaining offices that promote specified divisive concepts, from requiring or weighing diversity statements in hiring and admissions, and from compelling participation in DEI training. It also requires the State Department of Education, the Board of Trustees of State Institutions of Higher Learning and the Mississippi Community College Board to teach and promote the position that there are two genders, male and female, based on chromosomal makeup.

The attorney general and private parties can enforce the statute, and it calls for annual reporting. The lawsuit, filed June 9, 2025, was brought by teachers, professors, students and advocacy groups, who argued the law violates the First and Fourteenth Amendments. Wingate's first restraining order contained inaccuracies, including wrongly listed plaintiff names and mistakes about the bill's language. At oral argument, Circuit Judge Jerry Smith asked whether the court could be confident those errors had not affected the judge's ultimate reasoning.

In the ruling, the court wrote that the district court, or perhaps its AI agent if one wanted to be charitable, had ignored and manipulated governing law, apparently to satisfy a policy agenda. Wingate acknowledged in a letter that a law clerk used the AI tool Perplexity as a drafting assistant, and said the version docketed on July 20, 2025 was an early draft that had not gone through the court's standard review process. He sent the letter to Robert Conrad, director of the Administrative Office of the Courts, in response to an inquiry from Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley. Lawyers for Mississippi, including Anthony Shults of the attorney general's office, argued the errors undermined confidence in the court's legal reasoning and urged reassignment.

Plaintiffs' attorneys, led by Robert McDuff of the Mississippi Center for Justice, called the AI use a regrettable shortcut that did not affect the constitutionality question, and asked that the case stay with Wingate. The panel sided with the state. With the injunction vacated, the dispute returns to the district court under a new judge, and the constitutional questions the plaintiffs raised remain unresolved. Grassley's office has also flagged AI-related problems in orders from staff for a second federal judge, which the senator described as error-ridden.

stories.Headline: MS GOP asks Attorney General to investigate Colom campaign AI video - The Clarion-Ledger
stories.Summary:
On October 22, 2026, Mississippi Republican Party Chair Mike Hurst asked Attorney General Lynn Fitch to investigate an AI-generated video posted by Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom that depicts his opponent, Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, fleeing questions and photographs from reporters. The video, posted about a month before the November 3 election on Facebook and Instagram, carries the caption "Based on a true story," and the party says the content was not real. Hurst's request came in a letter to Fitch's office, and the Clarion-Ledger reported it that day. The following day, on Friday, October 23, Fitch notified Colom and his campaign to remove the ads from their social media platforms, according to WLBT.

The state law at issue was passed in 2024 and bars sharing realistic altered photos or videos, known as digitizations, within 90 days of an election with the intent to injure a candidate. Under WLBT's account, violations tied to an intent to deter voting can carry up to five years in prison and fines of up to $10,000. The Clarion-Ledger reported that the statute itself sets a penalty of up to a year in prison, a $5,000 fine or both, and it also contains exceptions for satire and parody without defining either term. Fitch's office told Colom to take down the video by 5 p.m. that Friday or face a possible injunction, and WLBT reported that as of late morning the video remained online.

Hurst argued in his letter and a news release that the video is deception rather than satire or parody, because Colom labeled it as a true story and did not disclose that it was artificial. He also pointed to an earlier simulated phone call Colom posted when he launched his campaign in 2025, which the party said it referred to the FBI, the Department of Justice and the U.S. Attorney, though the Clarion-Ledger reported it was unclear whether any penalties followed. Colom's campaign manager, Gerard Henderson, called the request an act of desperation and an attempt to weaponize public office, and said Republicans are worried about November 3. WLBT reported that Democratic analyst Brandon Jones called the legal filing political nonsense. The Clarion-Ledger also notes the race has grown increasingly bitter, with nicknames, dueling fake campaign websites and Hyde-Smith's earlier resurfacing of an arrest report about Colom, and that Colom campaigns with Kamala Harris on October 22 while Donald Trump is scheduled to rally for Hyde-Smith in Corinth on October 26.

stories.Headline: Pennsylvania one of the first states to require disclosures on AI-generated ads after Governor Josh Shapiro signs bill into law
stories.Summary:
Pennsylvania has become one of the first states to require disclosures on advertisements created with artificial intelligence. Governor Josh Shapiro signed the bill into law on Thursday, October 22, 2026. The measure is Senate Bill 806, also called the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act, and it was introduced and sponsored by Democratic state Senator Nick Pisciottano, who represents part of Allegheny County. The new rules take effect 60 days after the signing.

Under the law, any advertisement that includes images, video, audio or text that was generated or substantially rewritten by AI must carry a disclaimer saying so. That means an AI-made radio or TV commercial would have to include a note acknowledging how it was created. The law covers anything shown in Pennsylvania, even if it was produced out of state. Political ads are exempt from the requirement. Separately, Allegheny County Council unanimously approved a measure requiring county candidates to disclose AI-generated or altered campaign ads starting in January.

The Pennsylvania Office of Attorney General will enforce the law, with penalties for companies that break it. Pisciottano said the penalties could include a fine and even potential jail time, but that they would fall on AI companies rather than individual users, since the companies are responsible for adding the disclaimers as content is generated. He said the goal is to protect consumers from misleading ads and scams. While the bill was being drafted, he said, consumer groups representing older residents who are less comfortable with technology reported that their members were being scammed by fake AI advertising. KDKA reached out to one of the Republican co-sponsors and did not hear back.

Shapiro said in a social media post that the law is an important step but that more safeguards are needed, pointing to concerns about AI's effect on jobs, child safety and elections. Pisciottano noted that AI-generated ads are now common on Facebook, including images of food used by restaurants to promote their menus. He warned that the technology will keep improving until it is very hard to tell what is real from what is fake. Only a couple of other states have similar requirements, he said, and he expects the federal government or many other states to follow Pennsylvania's lead.

stories.Headline: OpenAI cuts valuation target by $150 bn to $1.25 tn | Why it has scaled back its funding ambitions ahead of IPO
stories.Summary:
OpenAI has lowered the valuation it is seeking from new investors by $150 billion, to $1.25 trillion, according to reports published on October 22 and 23, 2026. The company had discussed a figure of $1.4 trillion earlier in the talks, according to people familiar with the matter cited by Bloomberg. The cut reportedly followed resistance from some investors, though no reason for the lower figure was reported, and OpenAI declined to comment. Both numbers are pre-money prices, so they exclude the new capital being raised, and the discussions are ongoing, which means the final terms could still change.

The talks concern a funding round of up to $30 billion, with Coatue Management in talks to co-lead and investment funds from the United Arab Emirates, along with firms including BlackRock, also involved. Nothing has been signed, but OpenAI expects investor commitments to be finalised by the end of next week, and the final size of the round is still under discussion. OpenAI is also negotiating a separate deal to buy more computing capacity from the UAE. At $1.25 trillion, OpenAI would be the most valuable private company ever, and well above the $852 billion valuation it received in March, when it raised $122 billion from investors including Amazon, SoftBank and NVIDIA.

The revision comes as technology stocks fell this week after mixed quarterly results from companies including Meta Platforms and Tesla, which added to investor scrutiny of how much is being spent on artificial intelligence. On Thursday the Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.60% to 26,008.86, its steepest fall since early June. Microsoft, OpenAI's largest listed backer, fell 2.23% to $521.08 that day, then edged up 0.18% in after-hours trading. Microsoft valued its stake in OpenAI at about $135 billion after the October 2025 restructuring, roughly 27 percent on an as-converted diluted basis, though the March round has likely diluted that share and no updated figure has been disclosed. Microsoft reports fiscal first-quarter results on October 28.

On the question of going public, OpenAI confidentially filed its prospectus with the US Securities and Exchange Commission in June but has not disclosed a listing date. Chief financial officer Sarah Friar told employees in August that the company "will be a public company in 2027," while chief executive Sam Altman said the following month that listing at that point would be "an ill-advised moment." The IPO has been pushed back to next year, with the company citing its focus on AI safety efforts. Rival Anthropic is preparing an IPO expected next month, reportedly seeking a valuation of $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion after raising $65 billion in May at a $965 billion valuation, and OpenAI reportedly wants its commitments in place before Anthropic's filings make the two easier to compare. Separately, Chinese AI startup DeepSeek has raised about 100 billion yuan, or $14.98 billion, from investors including GigaDevice, Meituan and Geely, doubling its original target of 50 billion yuan.

stories.Headline: UAE's G42 signs pacts to explore AI infrastructure in Greece
stories.Summary:
Abu Dhabi's G42 and five of its portfolio companies signed initial agreements with Greek public and private partners on Friday, October 23, 2026, to explore AI infrastructure in Greece. The pacts were signed in Athens during an official visit by Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, at the UAE-Greece Strategic Forum. They were part of 18 memorandums of understanding, agreements and commercial partnerships between the two countries, valued at €12.75 billion, or $14.3 billion. G42's agreements cover AI infrastructure, government services, life sciences and smart cities, and they extend what the company calls its Intelligence Grid into Greece. That grid spans the full AI value chain, from data centres and advanced compute to cloud infrastructure and industry-specific applications.

Under agreements with Greece's Copelouzos Group, Khazna Data Centres and Core42 will explore building an AI factory in the country. Khazna would lead development of the physical infrastructure, while Core42 would supply cloud and AI compute capabilities for organisations in banking, telecoms, shipping and government. G42's subsidiary Presight will work with Greece's Ministry of Digital Governance on AI-powered analytics for urban mobility and municipal operations, starting with agentic AI for waste management and water network monitoring. Inception42 will also work with the ministry, which is formally called the Ministry of Digital Governance and Artificial Intelligence, on using agentic AI across government and education. That includes tools to support cabinet meetings and track progress against government priorities, training for officials to work with AI agents, and AI tutors and learning platforms.

In life sciences, M42 signed an initial pact with Athens LifeTech Park, known as ALTP, covering research, genomics sequencing infrastructure, population genomics, clinical development and the linking of institutional biobanks. The work is aimed at biomarker research in oncology, rare genetic diseases and neuroscience. The deal also sets up a two-way programme in which UAE life sciences start-ups get a base at the ALTP Incubator to enter the European market, while Greek and European ventures gain access to the UAE through M42's network. Mansoor Al Mansoori, chief executive of G42 International, said the agreements mark an important milestone in expanding the Intelligence Grid across Europe, and that G42 would work with trusted local partners in line with European standards.

Christos Copelouzos, chief executive of Copelouzos Group, said the partnership strengthens Greece's position as a digital and energy hub in South-east Europe, and that the AI factory would support the digital transformation of the Greek economy, attract investment and create highly skilled jobs. Greece's Minister of Digital Governance and Artificial Intelligence, Dimitris Papastergiou, said AI can make cities smarter, more efficient and safer, and that the collaboration with Presight will look at smart-city uses and ways to improve safety on public transport. Thomas Pramotedham, chief executive of Presight, said cities produce huge amounts of data whose value lies in turning it into intelligence that improves daily life. Ashish Koshy, chief executive of Inception42, said the programmes will follow European standards for Responsible AI. The agreements are initial and exploratory, and the articles do not give further timelines, though G42 has been helping other countries build domestic AI capabilities, including a framework agreement signed in February with a Vietnamese consortium.

stories.Headline: Sources: Anthropic and London-based PE firm Hg agree to launch a consultancy by the end of 2026 to embed AI consultants and engineers into European businesses (Financial Times)
stories.Summary:
Anthropic and the London-based private equity firm Hg have agreed to create an independent consultancy that will place AI consultants and engineers inside European businesses, according to a report from the Financial Times that cited unnamed sources. PYMNTS relayed the report on Friday, October 23, 2026. The new company is expected to launch by the end of the year. Neither Anthropic nor Hg immediately replied to PYMNTS' request for comment, and the Techmeme item summarizing the story offers no further detail.

The reported plan calls for the consultancy to have hubs in London and Berlin. Its job would be to help European firms deploy artificial intelligence, with staff working directly inside client companies rather than advising from outside. The articles give no figures for funding, ownership stakes or headcount. They also do not name who will run the new company.

The two companies already have a track record together. Hg said in September that it was extending its existing collaboration with Anthropic to bring agentic AI capabilities to the companies in its portfolio. That relationship had already run for three years, covering a joint AI hackathon series and staff enablement inside Hg's own business. Hg co-CEOs Steve Batchelor and JB Brian said at the time that Hg backed the shift toward agentic AI early and that the Anthropic relationship is central to it. They added that they want portfolio companies to have a direct line to the frontier of the technology and are keen to deepen the tie.

The move fits a wider pattern of Anthropic working through finance partners to get its Claude model into large companies. In May, Anthropic partnered with Goldman Sachs, Blackstone and Hellman & Friedman on a venture that helps enterprise customers embed Claude in their operations. Anthropic's chief financial officer, Krishna Rao, said then that partnerships with leading systems integrators are central to how Claude reaches large enterprises, and that the new firm would add operating capability and capital from alternative asset managers. Reports from May also showed monthly job listings for forward-deployed engineers rising by more than 800% between January and September 2025, a sign of how quickly companies are hiring for roles that put AI systems to work inside enterprises. The next step is the launch the sources say is planned before the end of 2026.

stories.Headline: SK Hyper Seeks $350 Billion for First 5GW Phase of 15GW AI Data Center Plan
stories.Summary:
SK Hyper, the AI data center arm of SK Telecom, said it is seeking about $350 billion, or 463 trillion won, to fund the first 5-gigawatt phase of a plan to build 15 gigawatts of data center capacity in South Korea. Chief executive Chung Suk-keun laid out the strategy on October 23 during an appearance on Bloomberg TV's "Bloomberg Tech: Asia." The goal is to draw global companies' AI infrastructure into the country and capture computing demand from elsewhere in Asia, including Japan and Taiwan. The company hopes this will turn South Korea into a global AI infrastructure hub.

The plan calls for 15GW of capacity by 2035, with phased operations starting in 2029 to reach the initial 5GW. The $350 billion estimate for that first phase includes servers and other equipment. SK Hyper intends to build a cluster of more than 2GW in the Yeongnam region, beginning with its AI data center in Ulsan, and to add gigawatt-scale facilities in the Chungcheong and southwestern regions. It aims to land its first outside investment late this year or early next year, then raise more money over the following three to four years, sharing the total cost with data center customers and outside investors. SK Telecom has previously said it would invest up to 750 billion won in SK Hyper in stages through 2030.

Chung said he does not expect much difficulty securing power and sites for the first 5GW, and that the biggest challenges will be securing real demand in the global market and raising the capital needed. He explained that South Korea's data center market is currently about 1GW, which has made the country unattractive in the global industry until now, and that the initial 5GW is roughly five times that figure. For this reason, SK Hyper is talking with global hyperscalers about bringing AI inference hubs to Korea and wants to attract training computing infrastructure as well. According to Bloomberg, Chung said revenue could begin as early as next year, ahead of 2029, when the first data centers are scheduled for completion.

Chung argued that actual computing demand remains firm despite a recent pullback in AI infrastructure stocks and weaker investor sentiment, saying AI model developers and service providers see customer demand rising sharply. He said the company should prepare in advance rather than wait for demand to appear, while managing risk by confirming demand with big tech firms and hyperscalers before investing. He also said the competitive edge has shifted from who holds the most graphics processing units to who can generate tokens at the lowest cost with the highest efficiency. SK Hyper plans to combine SK Group's semiconductor, energy and telecommunications strengths, and Chung added that many countries want sovereign AI infrastructure they can control at home, a trend he expects to spread. Expansion from 5GW to 15GW will depend on global customer demand.

stories.Headline: Microsoft’s AI diagnostic tool outperforms general physicians in complex cases, study finds
stories.Summary:
Microsoft researchers have reported that an AI system they built diagnosed complex medical cases more accurately than practicing generalist physicians, according to a study published October 22, 2026 in Science. The system, called the Diagnostic Orchestrator, or DxO, runs on a commercial large language model, GPT-5 in the main results, and simulates a panel of physicians who track a differential diagnosis, challenge leading hypotheses and weigh the cost of each test. On 304 New England Journal of Medicine clinicopathological conference cases it reached the correct diagnosis 83.2% of the time, versus 36.1% for generalist physicians who could use search and reference tools. On 325 emergency department admissions drawn from the MIMIC-IV-ED database, it scored 80.3%, against 46.8% for physicians.

The study built a benchmark called SDBench, in which each case begins with a brief clinical vignette and the diagnostician must decide what history to take, which tests to order and when to commit to a diagnosis. A separate AI gatekeeper released information only when asked, and test costs were estimated from hospital chargemaster pricing. Physicians averaged 22.3% accuracy without reference tools, and the best individual physician reached 51.8% on the conference cases and 62.5% on the emergency cases. Physicians asked 5.6 questions on average before ordering a first test, while DxO asked 25.5. Without budget limits, DxO's testing cost more than the physicians' ($5,431 versus $4,725 on the conference cases, $4,979 versus $3,400 on the emergency cases), but budget-limited versions scored 80.9% at $2,241 and 79.6% at $1,303 on the conference cases, and 73.2% at $2,634 and 69.5% at $2,037 on the emergency cases.

All 15 authors are Microsoft employees, including Microsoft AI chief executive Mustafa Suleyman, Dominic King and Eric Horvitz, and they hold equity in the company, which sells AI and health care services. Eight authors are named inventors on a Microsoft patent application tied to the evaluation framework, and the study had no outside funding. The authors argue that static benchmarks, which hand over a full case write-up at once, can overstate AI ability because they cannot show whether a system asks the right questions, avoids needless testing or knows when to stop. They suggested the AI's edge may come from its breadth of knowledge and its consistency, without fatigue, time pressure or cognitive bias.

The authors acknowledged limits. The comparison was against individual generalists, not specialists or teams, and they expect the gap to narrow against specialists matched to each case. The NEJM cases are chosen for teaching value, the benchmark was text-only with no imaging or pathology slides, and every case had a pathological diagnosis, so healthy and benign visits were left out. Cost estimates used standardized U.S. pricing, and the study did not assess treatment, patient safety or outcomes. Next, the authors plan to design workflows in which clinicians and AI work together, and see potential uses in medical education and continuing professional development.

stories.Headline: India's Tech Mahindra partners with SpaceXSI for AI-powered software development - CNA
stories.Summary:
Tech Mahindra, the Indian IT services company, announced on Thursday, October 22, that it has partnered with SpaceXSI to use artificial intelligence to modernise legacy applications and speed up software development. Reuters-style coverage described Tech Mahindra as India's fifth-largest IT firm. The company will also bring in the chatbot Grok Build to set up industry-specific solutions. The announcement did not say when the joint offering will become available.

The deal combines Tech Mahindra's engineering and enterprise transformation services with SpaceXSI's development platform. The two sides plan to concentrate on software delivery, code quality and developer productivity across technology, telecommunications, banking and financial services, manufacturing, healthcare and retail. They also intend to run joint go-to-market initiatives, customer engagements and industry-specific programmes. Tech Mahindra will set up enablement and certification programmes to help client engineering teams adopt the tools.

Toni Adams, Head of Global Partnerships at SpaceXSI, said in the announcement that most enterprises already accept that AI will change how software is built. What they lack, she said, is expertise in rolling it out across large and varied engineering teams without breaking what already works. Tech Mahindra said it will fold Grok Build expertise into its engineering transformation and application modernisation services. The companies described the offering as designed for enterprise settings, where governance, security and compliance are requirements.

Tech Mahindra already has similar pacts with Google Gemini and Microsoft, but this is the first time an Indian IT major has teamed up with the AI division of rocket maker SpaceX. The company did not name any customer deployments, disclose financial terms or put a figure on expected productivity gains. It has also not said how much revenue, if any, it expects the collaboration to bring in. Separately, Tech Mahindra plans to report its AI revenue on its own starting in the second half of fiscal 2027.

stories.Headline: OpenAI, Anthropic, and Nvidia had record lobbying quarters
stories.Summary:
Nvidia, Anthropic and OpenAI each had their highest-spending lobbying quarter yet between July and September, according to federal disclosures reported by The Verge on October 22, 2026. Nvidia spent the most, at $2.2 million, followed by Anthropic at $2.1 million and OpenAI at $1.5 million. Together, the three companies spent nearly $6 million on issues including cybersecurity and child safety. Apple also set a record that quarter, spending $3.1 million, its first quarter above $3 million.

The disclosures give some detail on what each firm pressed Washington about. Anthropic listed AI-related provisions in the Kids Online Safety Act, export control provisions in the AI Overwatch Act, an executive order from Trump renaming AI "Super Intelligence," and the Ratepayer Protection Act, which would put data center energy costs on their developers. OpenAI lobbied Congress, the White House, the Small Business Administration and the Commerce and State Departments on cybersecurity evaluations for frontier models, AI safety oversight frameworks and antitrust protections for information sharing, along with copyright. Nvidia lobbied Congress, federal agencies and White House offices on 6G networks, "responsible AI design," competition policy, quantum computing and export controls. Apple engaged on intellectual property, tariffs, kids online safety, competition and domestic chip manufacturing, including bills that would make app stores verify users' ages.

The companies themselves are not quoted in the coverage, and the filings list only high-level topics. The Verge's reporter, Lauren Feiner, notes that OpenAI's lobbying looks like a response to fallout from the Hugging Face attack, though the disclosures do not say so directly. She also points out that the sums are not unusual next to older Big Tech players: Microsoft has spent at least $2 million a quarter since 2021, and Google regularly spends more than $3 million. What stands out, in her telling, is how quickly the three AI firms have ramped up.

The growth is sharp when compared with earlier years. OpenAI did not spend even $1 million in a single quarter until this year, and did not top half a million until the end of 2024. The most Anthropic spent in one quarter last year was just over $1 million, and this is the first quarter Nvidia has passed $2 million. The spending came as tech CEOs attended a White House lunch with President Donald Trump in late September, which produced a "morally binding" AI safety accord, and just before Trump named his AI czar and task force. With Democrats expected to win back at least some control of Congress in this year's midterms, the article suggests AI companies may find it even more important to engage lawmakers who see cracking down on the industry as a winning issue, and that lobbying will likely keep growing whichever party holds power next year.

stories.Headline: Harvard College students are using newly expanded access to Anthropic’s Claude for coursework, extracurricular projects, and personal tasks after the Faculty of Arts and Sciences began providing institutional access to the AI platform this summer. The FAS fir
stories.Summary:
Harvard College students are using newly widened access to Anthropic's Claude for coursework, extracurricular projects and personal tasks, according to the Harvard Crimson. The Faculty of Arts and Sciences began providing institutional access to the AI platform this summer. The change was first announced in April, when the FAS said it would add Claude to its suite of available AI tools while moving ChatGPT Edu to a request-only basis. The handover of tool availability to Harvard affiliates took place over the summer, and students are now in their first semester with the FAS-sponsored access.

Students described a wide range of uses. In General Education 1201, on neuroscience and artificial intelligence, Claude is built into the syllabus and assignments, which Iris A. Heikkinen '29 said teaches students how to use AI for studying. Leonardo Miranda '30 is using it in a first-year seminar called "Letting Claude Cook," where students must use the tool for a class project, and he said there is no cap on how many credits a student can use. Santiago D. Revilla '30 built a website that pulls in his Google Calendar and shows the weather for each day so he can plan walks and runs, while Ankit Biswas '30, a research fellow at the Cambridge Boston Align Initiative, uses Claude to scaffold ideas and handle implementation. Sean "Brady" Merrill '30 said he has used Claude Premium to help build models for a racing boat club he belongs to.

Responsibility for the rollout rests with the FAS, which made the April announcement and oversaw the summer transition. The seminar Miranda described is taught by Douglas P. Finkbeiner, the FAS's senior adviser on generative AI, who previously worked for Anthropic. Some students tied their preference for Claude to their views of the company. Merrill said he favors it because Anthropic's leadership and staff did not sign a deal with the Pentagon, a reference to a dispute earlier this year between Anthropic and the Department of Defense over AI safety safeguards. Conner M. Lewandowski '30 said he would rather support a company whose vision for AI and moral outlook match his own.

The Harvard access sits alongside a broader push by Anthropic into academia, including a new Guest Investigators program reported by Tech Times. The company opened a call on Wednesday for principal investigators at academic institutions, nonprofits and government labs to apply for embedded research collaborations lasting 8 to 12 weeks, with extensions possible for some projects. The program covers five life sciences areas, including causal human biology, drug discovery and clinical science, and excludes private companies and startups. Anthropic pays all model-compute costs, and researchers keep their data and the right to pursue follow-on work, while Anthropic commits to open-sourcing accompanying code and data and to publishing results jointly. The application window runs about 14 days from October 22, 2026, and Anthropic has said it will try to notify selected participants roughly 14 days after applications close.

stories.Headline: Sri Lanka launches UNESCO’s AI Readiness Assessment Methodology (RAM)
stories.Summary:
UNESCO's Regional Office for South Asia, working with Sri Lanka's Ministry of Digital Economy, has launched the organization's Readiness Assessment Methodology on artificial intelligence in the country. The first meeting of the National Steering Committee took place in Colombo on 20 May 2026, and a second followed on 2 September 2026. UNESCO announced the launch on 22 October 2026. Sri Lanka is one of the first few countries to run the exercise using RAM 2.0, an updated version of the original method. The tool gives a structured picture of whether a country is ready to develop and use AI in a responsible, ethical and inclusive way, and it supports the Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence.

The Steering Committee guides the assessment and is meant to make sure it captures the full complexity of Sri Lanka's AI ecosystem across every area RAM covers. Its members include other government agencies, the Sri Lanka National Commission for UNESCO, private sector leaders, experts from academia and civil society, and Citra Lab at the United Nations Development Programme. Several multi-stakeholder consultations are planned over the coming months in Colombo, Jaffna, Kandy, Batticaloa and Galle. LIRNEasia, a Colombo-based economic and digital policy think tank, has been brought in as the national implementation partner. The exercise will produce a report to complement the country's digital transformation agenda and the proposed national AI strategy, offering practical recommendations for a human-centred AI ecosystem that reflects international standards.

The committee is chaired by Waruna Sri Dhanapala, Secretary of the Ministry of Digital Economy, and Eunsong Kim, Chief of Social and Human Sciences at the UNESCO Regional Office for South Asia. At the meetings, participants noted that AI and its ethical use are a priority for the Government of Sri Lanka. They also stressed that policymaking in this area should be inclusive and draw on a wide range of voices across society. UNESCO says the committee's main job is to steer the assessment so that it reflects those realities.

The wider backdrop is a push on digital infrastructure, since another report says Sri Lanka has only around 5 megawatts of data center capacity and officials estimate it needs 25 to 50 megawatts of cloud and AI computing capacity in the short term. The government is seeking Chinese support for a National Sovereign AI Computing Centre, and the two countries are working toward a memorandum of understanding on AI cooperation. Dr. Hans Wijayasuriya, Chief Presidential Adviser on the Digital Economy, said the government will step in on data center and cloud investment because private suppliers have not yet responded enough to demand. Globally, UNESCO had deployed RAM in more than 75 Member States as of August 2026, with the process complete in 60, including India, Bangladesh and Maldives in South Asia.

stories.Headline: Ukrainian drone strikes hit five Russian data centers, disrupting cloud services and AI work
stories.Summary:
Ukrainian drones struck five Russian data centers this month, the Associated Press reported on October 22, 2026, and experts expect the damage to take months, perhaps years, to repair. Three of the sites belong to Yandex, Russia's largest technology company, one to Sberbank, the country's biggest bank, and one serves VKontakte, its main social network. The first strike, on October 8, hit a Yandex data center in Sasovo, in the Ryazan region, which houses two of the company's three supercomputers. Yandex sites in Kaluga and Vladimir followed on October 9 and October 11, then Sberbank's data center and AI hub in Balakovo, in the Saratov region, on October 14. Four days later a data center in Saint Petersburg serving VKontakte was hit.

Yandex, Sberbank and VKontakte have said little about the damage, but people and businesses across Russia reported lasting interruptions to cloud services. Banking, online shopping, maps and ride hailing were hit, along with Yandex's voice assistant Alisa and AI chatbots, and arbitration courts reportedly called off or delayed hearings after losing access to databases. One Moscow resident told the AP he could not collect an online order, and a taxi driver said he lost fares because the Yandex app would not connect him with passengers. Yandex said it restored most of its key cloud services within days by shifting work to its other Russian data centers. The company had rehearsed losing one of its six data centers, but not three in four days.

The heavier blow is to Russia's AI work. Yandex's three supercomputers, which it uses to build its models, rank among the world's 500 most powerful, and the one at Sasovo was ranked 19th. Satellite images pointed to serious damage, and observers said fires probably ruined high-end chips and other equipment. Mikhail Klimarev, head of the Internet Protection Society, an activist group, told the AP the strikes leave Russia far behind in the AI race, and that sanctions and a global chip shortage could make repairs slow, costly or impossible. Connor Martin, an analyst cited by the AP, wrote that Russia will struggle to replace the American-designed chips inside the Yandex machines.

The attacks follow Russian strikes on data centers in Ukraine that disrupted internet and television services, part of a wider campaign by each side against the other's infrastructure. Ukraine has hit Russian oil refineries and the warehouses of the online retailers Wildberries and Ozon. Nick Reiners, a senior analyst at Eurasia Group, said Russia lacks the air defenses to cover so large a country, and that its rule keeping data inside its borders has made that data easier to knock out. Iranian drones earlier hit two Amazon Web Services data centers in the United Arab Emirates and one in Bahrain, and AWS said last month it could not restore access to resources and data at two of them. Klimarev expects many Russian companies to rent computing capacity in Europe as a result.

stories.Headline: LG Electronics to Bring Robots, AI to World's Largest Tidal Power Plant
stories.Summary:
LG Electronics signed a memorandum of understanding with Korea Water Resources Corporation, known as K-water, on Oct. 22 at the Sihwa Tidal Culture Center in Ansan, Gyeonggi Province. The agreement covers the Sihwa Lake tidal power plant, which has the largest generation capacity of any tidal plant in the world. The two sides agreed to turn the facility into an AI-powered smart plant, applying digital twins and robots on site. They also agreed to cooperate on research and development, policy and expansion abroad.

The company will first use digital twin technology to copy the whole plant in a virtual space and link it to real-time data from generation equipment and closed-circuit cameras. That setup is meant to allow forecasts of power output, testing of operating scenarios and diagnosis of equipment conditions. LG is also considering an AI agent built on Exaone, the proprietary model from LG AI Research, to analyze output losses, spot equipment faults, support predictive maintenance, assess risks and tune inspection schedules. For work on site, patrol robots, AI-equipped cameras and industrial robots would handle facility patrols, equipment inspections, monitoring of hazardous areas, and the storage and transport of spare parts.

Lee Seung-ki, head of LG Electronics' Smart Factory Solution Center, said it is significant that skills built on manufacturing floors are now being applied to public infrastructure. He said the company will work with K-water to support the plant's digital transformation and keep improving its operating efficiency and safety. The Korea Times reported the company's statement in similar terms. LG framed the project as a reference case for taking its smart factory solutions into energy infrastructure at home and overseas.

The deal marks the first time LG has carried smart factory technology from manufacturing into public infrastructure such as power plants, according to The Elec. The company wants to grow beyond its existing manufacturing and logistics clients and join energy projects led by governments and large corporations. Cumulative orders for its smart factory solutions business passed 1 trillion won in the first half of 2026, two years after the unit's launch. The articles describe the digital twin, AI agent and robotics work as items to be examined or tested, and they give no timeline or cost for the upgrades.

stories.Headline: How Governments Worldwide Are Shaping What AI Can Say About Politics
stories.Summary:
Governments around the world are increasingly shaping what AI chatbots can say about politics, according to a piece by Jordi Calvet-Bademunt, a researcher at a nonpartisan think tank at Vanderbilt University who studies free speech policy. It was republished by Honolulu Civil Beat from The Conversation on October 23, 2026. He notes that about 1 in 5 voters has asked chatbots about elections and politics ahead of the U.S. midterms, and that because many tech companies apply the same policies worldwide, answers American voters get may be influenced by governments at home and abroad. He and colleagues worked with global legal experts on two reports, published in 2025 and 2026, covering how governments in 12 countries and regions regulate AI.

Their research found that governments often rely on existing rules, such as national security or anti-state propaganda laws, rather than new AI laws. In 2024, an Indian journalist asked Google's Gemini whether Prime Minister Narendra Modi's policies were fascist, and the chatbot said some experts say yes. India then required official permission before "unreliable" AI models could be released, though it later dropped the requirement. China requires models to uphold "socialist core values," and a Turkish court blocked Grok posts that allegedly insulted President Erdoğan, Atatürk and religious values. In December 2025, a Vietnamese court sentenced two activists living in Germany to 17 years each in prison for spreading anti-state material, after prosecutors accused them of using AI to fake voices and images of Vietnamese leaders.

Some rules reach across borders. The European Union's AI Act, adopted in 2024, requires any company offering AI tools in Europe to mark AI-generated content, and Anthropic applies the marks globally because it cannot reliably do so by region. In August 2026, the EU placed ChatGPT under the strictest tier of its Digital Services Act, so OpenAI must assess and reduce systemic risks, including risks to elections such as disinformation. The Dutch Data Protection Authority tested four chatbots before the 2025 national election, found that the political middle ground "virtually disappears" in their voting advice, and urged providers to stop their systems being used for it. In 2024, Thierry Breton, then the EU's top digital rules enforcer, reminded Elon Musk of his legal obligations before Musk's live interview with Donald Trump on X.

The author argues the United States is no exception. President Trump's 2025 executive order on "Preventing Woke AI in the Federal Government" requires AI models the government buys to be "truth-seeking" and ideologically neutral, a term the author says can mean very different things to different people. The Federal Trade Commission has suggested that AI companies steering answers toward undisclosed ideological objectives might break consumer protection law. Dozens of states have passed laws restricting AI-generated political deepfakes, and California and Hawaii banned sharing deceptive AI content about candidates in the months around an election, but U.S. courts blocked both laws on First Amendment grounds. The author advises voters to treat chatbot answers on elections as a starting point and not to let them replace their own critical thinking at the ballot box.

stories.Headline: Schneider Electric Unveils Modular Power Systems for AI Data Centers
stories.Summary:
Schneider Electric announced on October 23 that it has unveiled new Prefabricated Power Modules and Power Skids for AI data centers, both built on a reference design it co-developed with Nvidia. The company says the factory-built approach lets operators put power infrastructure in place in as little as six months. Demand for electricity at data centers is climbing as high-performance GPUs are deployed, and power supply capacity has become a key competitive factor. Instead of installing individual pieces of equipment on site, operators can use standardized modules made in advance to shorten construction time.

The reference design targets Nvidia's GB300 NVL72 system and supports power density of up to 142 kilowatts per rack. It also ties power management together with liquid cooling controls. The power modules use Schneider's Galaxy VXL uninterruptible power supply technology and come in capacities of 2 megawatts, 2.25 megawatts and 2.5 megawatts. The 2.5-megawatt version is the largest single-container prefabricated power solution the company has released so far. Capacity can be expanded by adding modules, so operators can build for initial demand and scale up in stages as they add GPU servers.

A Schneider Electric official said that securing the necessary power infrastructure quickly and reliably is critical to scaling AI data centers. The official added that by applying the design developed with Nvidia, the company aims to help customers handle high-density AI environments and expand their equipment as power needs shift. Schneider plans to supply the products to large hyperscale facilities, to neoclouds that provide AI-dedicated cloud services, and to colocation data centers that host servers for multiple companies. It also expects to serve sites that need large power capacity, such as clusters for training AI models.

The products will be designed, manufactured and tested at the company's facility in Sant Boi de Llobregat, near Barcelona, Spain, which it recently expanded to meet rising demand for modular data center infrastructure. They will launch first in Europe, with supply widening to North America during 2026 and then rolling out to other regions, including Asia-Pacific. Separately, a day earlier, Schneider announced a collaboration with Nvidia and HPE to bring AI to process industries, introducing what it calls Industrial AI Agents at the Edge, built on HPE Private Cloud AI. That effort focuses on operational technology monitoring, cybersecurity and energy optimization rather than data center power.

stories.Headline: Kansas City lab to train AI to predict protein changes tied to ALS, Alzheimer’s
stories.Summary:
A Kansas City research lab has been chosen to take part in a $28.6 million national effort to train artificial intelligence to predict protein changes linked to neurodegenerative disease. KCTV reported the news on October 21, 2026. Investigator Randal Halfmann and a team of local scientists at the Stowers Institute for Medical Research received a $4.1 million grant as their share of the project. They will use technology in new ways to help predict harmful protein changes tied to Alzheimer's, Huntington's and ALS.

Halfmann's lab will produce more than 10 billion measurements covering 50,000 proteins and over a million samples. This data is meant to teach AI to recognize the moment when something begins to go wrong. The task is hard because AI can readily detect many proteins but struggles with those involved in diseases such as Alzheimer's, which keep changing shape. The microscopic protein clumping under study will be collected at a level of detail never achieved before.

Halfmann said the question behind the work has motivated biology for roughly 60 years. He believes the effort will lay groundwork for generations, and his ultimate aim is to predict when a person will develop a disease and how quickly it will progress. He expects the data to create a much larger pool of people entering clinical trials, which would give those trials the power to find therapies that work. He also said he is optimistic that in two years researchers will be in a much better position to act.

His team has been working on this problem for years, and in 2023 the Stowers lab first identified the molecular trigger behind toxic protein buildup in Huntington's disease. With millions of Americans affected by neurodegenerative disease, Halfmann said the situation creates a sense of urgency, and he does not take any day for granted because every day matters to patients. The $28.6 million effort brings together select scientists from a handful of top institutions and universities around the country. KCTV pointed readers to the project's website for more on this and other research.

The list was published that day by the Markets Daily site, under the byline of Michael Walen. The companies were picked because they had the highest dollar trading volume of any AI stocks over the last several days. A similar list appeared on October 20th on the Ticker Report site, written by Ethan Ryder, and it carried three of the same names plus two others.

The October 22nd list describes each company briefly. Hut 8 builds and runs data centers for digital asset mining, computing and AI in the United States, and it reports in four segments: Digital Assets Mining, Managed Services, High Performance Computing Colocation and Cloud, and Other. Tempus AI applies artificial intelligence to precision medicine, giving physicians tools for personalized care while also supporting the discovery and delivery of therapeutics. SentinelOne is a cybersecurity provider whose Singularity Platform uses AI to prevent, detect and respond to threats across endpoints, cloud workloads and identity credentials. Appian offers a low-code platform covering AI, process automation, data fabric and process mining, while Upstart runs a cloud-based AI lending platform for personal loans, auto loans, home equity lines of credit and small dollar loans, connecting borrowers with banks and credit unions.

The earlier list, covering October 19th, kept Hut 8, Tempus AI and SentinelOne, and swapped in Ambarella and Exyn Technologies for Appian and Upstart. Ambarella designs semiconductors for high-definition and ultra HD video compression, image processing and AI vision. Exyn Technologies describes itself as a pioneer in autonomous robotics and AI for complex environments where GPS is unavailable. Both articles were produced by MarketBeat's screener, which means the selections come from a trading-volume ranking rather than from an editorial judgment about the companies' prospects.

The articles define AI stocks as shares of public companies that develop, provide or heavily use technologies such as machine learning, data analytics, robotics and AI-enabled software and hardware. They note that such stocks can give investors exposure to the growth of the AI industry, but that performance can be affected by competition, regulation, high valuations and the fast pace of technological change. The pieces say nothing about what any of the five companies will do next, and they report no price moves or analyst ratings. stories.Summary:
Artificial Intelligence Technology Solutions, Inc. (OTCID: AITX), the Detroit-based AI security company, reported results for its fiscal second quarter ended August 31, 2026, in a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission on October 20, 2026, and announced them on October 21. The company said revenue returned to sequential and year-over-year growth and that its customer base is more diversified than at any point in its history. It also said an expanded cost program targets monthly operating cash breakeven in January 2027. A day later, on October 22, it announced that its subsidiary Robotic Assistance Devices, Inc. (RAD) had secured recent orders for twelve devices across its RIO Mini, ROSA and TOM product lines, covering construction, commercial property and logistics uses.

Revenue for the quarter was $1,985,604, up 5% from $1,888,749 a year earlier and up 8% from $1,831,202 in the first quarter of fiscal 2027. Device rental revenue rose 4% to $1,765,293, and direct sales rose 14% to $220,311. Revenue excluding the largest customer hit a record $1,627,444, up 61% from $1,010,243 a year earlier and up 11% from $1,463,319 in the first quarter, beating a sequential growth outlook of more than 10% given in July. The largest customer, which began cutting its spend in December 2025 as part of its own cost reductions, contributed $358,160, down 3% sequentially and 18% of total revenue, compared with 46% a year earlier. Recurring rental revenue made up 89% of the total, an annualized run-rate of about $7.1 million.

Gross profit was $1,063,301, or 54% of revenue, after a non-cash inventory write-down of $270,987 tied to the discontinued residential camera line. Without the write-down, gross profit was $1,334,288, or 67% of revenue, against 71% a year earlier and 65% in the first quarter. Operating expenses for the six months ended August 31 fell 5% to $7,636,884 from $8,066,193, and general and administrative costs dropped 6%, or $380,193, mainly because of lower salary and wage expense. The company noted these figures include only one month of the cost-reduction program announced on August 3, 2026. The results are reviewed but unaudited.

On the orders, a longstanding channel partner ordered five ROSA units for a Midwest construction site, a security services partner ordered three ROSA units for customer projects including commercial property security, and an existing construction customer ordered two RIO Mini units for separate sites. An existing global logistics customer ordered two more TOM units for visitor management in facility lobbies. Troy McCanna, RAD's Chief Security Officer and Chief Revenue Officer, said orders like these are becoming routine, that customers are adding devices and partners are bringing RAD into more projects, and that every deployment is a chance to earn the next order. The company cautioned that orders do not confirm delivery, revenue recognition or positive cash flow, and that its filings describe a history of operating losses and going-concern risk.

stories.Headline: Google DeepMind Staff Resign Over Military AI Contracts
stories.Summary:
Several Google DeepMind researchers have resigned or are reportedly preparing to leave over the company's expanding military work, according to BBC interviews with current and former staff. The departures follow Reuters reporting that Google signed a classified agreement with the US Department of Defense allowing its AI models to be used for "any lawful government purpose," including classified military work. Sofia Liguori, a London-based research engineer who joined DeepMind in 2023, resigned this week, and the Intercept published an interview with her on October 21. Researcher Andreas Kirsch also resigned separately, saying Google's governance and oversight structures were not strong enough for safe deployment in military and classified settings. The Pentagon agreement says the systems should not be used for domestic mass surveillance or for autonomous weapons without appropriate human oversight and control, according to Reuters.

Reuters also reported that the deal requires Google to help adjust its AI safety settings and filters at the government's request, which could allow some safeguards to be changed. Kirsch reportedly said Google may have little practical ability to monitor or veto how the Pentagon uses its technology once it sits inside classified systems. Liguori took a personal sick-out the day after Google announced the classified contract in April, and she told the Intercept she could no longer work for a company that would help kill people or make war's brutality easier to escalate. In an internal resignation letter, she urged colleagues to "stay human" and wrote that she no longer believed the technology would benefit society.

Google told the BBC that it applies a consistent contract-review process tied to its acceptable-use policies and AI principles, and that employees have ways to raise concerns without fear of retaliation. The company's published principles call for human oversight and alignment with international law and human rights. Liguori said she was dismayed by Google's work with the US and Israeli militaries, including the Project Nimbus cloud contract, which she learned about after the Gaza war escalated. Google has said Nimbus was not meant for sensitive military or intelligence work involving weapons or intelligence services.

Claims about AI-assisted targeting linked to that contract remain disputed, and an Israeli government minister rejected them in the documentary Naza as false and distorted. Google is not alone in pursuing such work, as the BBC reported that OpenAI, Amazon, Microsoft, SpaceX, Oracle, Nvidia and Reflection have also signed or sought US military AI arrangements. Nimbus, a $1.2 billion deal shared by Google and Amazon, has drawn separate criticism from employees over services provided to Israel's government and military. Retired Lt.

Gen. Jack Shanahan, who once led the Pentagon's Project Maven, warned the BBC that pressure to deploy can outpace careful testing and evaluation. Former OpenAI geopolitics head Sarah Shoker told the BBC that AI can shrink the time available for decisions, making it hard for a human to check hundreds of AI-selected targets for errors. The articles do not say whether more DeepMind staff will leave or whether Google will change the terms of the Pentagon agreement.

stories.Headline: Scaling Laws Roadshow at North Dakota Law: Justice Jerod Tufte on AI in the Judiciary
stories.Summary:
North Dakota's interim Artificial Intelligence and Data Center Committee voted on Tuesday to advance a proposal setting up AI consumer protections and a state Artificial Intelligence Council. The panel recommended the broader bill to Legislative Management after discussing concerns about privacy, enforcement and the makeup of the proposed council. It chose not to advance a separate companion chatbot bill as a committee measure, and instead agreed to keep refining it for possible introduction by an individual legislator before the 2027 session. Members stressed that the draft is still open to revision.

Under the broader proposal, AI systems dealing with consumers would have to disclose that users are talking with artificial intelligence. It would bar developing or deploying AI with the intent to encourage self-harm, harm to others or criminal activity, and would restrict certain uses of biometric data to identify people without consent. The attorney general would enforce these protections, and a supervised testing program would let developers try out innovative AI systems for a limited time without certain regulatory authorizations, with quarterly reports sent to the Information Technology Department. A seven-member AI council would study the technology and recommend changes to state laws. The chatbot draft would require bots to identify themselves at the start of each interaction and at least every three hours of continuous adult use, with hourly reminders for minors, plus crisis referrals and limits on manipulative tactics aimed at minors.

Representative Mary Schneider questioned language giving the attorney general exclusive enforcement power and blocking private lawsuits, saying parents or others harmed by AI may need to bring their own cases. Senator Janne Myrdal said those questions deserve more consideration during the session, calling the draft a good start but not a final bill. On data centers, Representative Anna Novak outlined a developing plan focused on electricity costs, water use and what happens when facilities close. Her "bring your own power" idea is meant to keep residential customers from paying costs tied to data centers, though differences between investor-owned utilities and rural electric cooperatives complicate it. She also proposed closed-loop water systems and standards for removing equipment, and said zoning would stay local, followed by state permitting.

Several members asked whether new rules should cover only data centers or all large industrial electricity users, and others objected to reclamation requirements not imposed on other industries. Senator Dean Rummel suggested narrowing data center sales tax exemptions to computer technology and ending them for items such as cooling systems, racks and fiber optics. The committee discussed these ideas without advancing a finished data center bill, and individual lawmakers are expected to develop proposals for the next session. Separately, a North Dakota Monitor report on the attorney general race noted that the 2025 Legislature banned possession of computer-generated child sexual abuse images and required a disclaimer on AI used in political ads. Republican Attorney General Drew Wrigley and Democrat Tim Lamb both said AI should not replace humans in investigations or legal work.

stories.Headline: Some government websites taken down in response to security risk: AI minister
stories.Summary:
Some Canadian government websites were taken down temporarily on Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026, as a precaution against a security risk, Artificial Intelligence Minister Evan Solomon said. He announced the move in a social media post, saying the sites went dark to protect government systems and Canadians' information. The decision followed guidance from the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security. Solomon did not appear to say, in the portions of the reports that could be read, which sites were affected.

The reports say the shutdown was a response to a vulnerability found in PHP, a widely used programming language. The cyber division of the FBI said the flaw could let malicious actors remotely run code in that language, which could put sensitive data and networks at risk. The PHP Foundation, which includes developers who work on the language, said it has released fixes for the vulnerabilities, along with instructions on how to update systems. Solomon described the problem as a global issue and said other governments and organizations are also taking measures.

Solomon said affected federal websites will be restored once patches are applied, and that the government is taking the matter seriously. He told reporters that Canada's response was part of a broader effort to protect its digital systems. The British Columbia government also posted on social media on Wednesday that it had taken some of its web pages offline as a precaution following a new global cybersecurity vulnerability. It is unclear whether the risk is the same one Solomon described, but the B.C. government said its teams were working to fix the problem.

The website of the Finnish government was only partly available on Wednesday. A message to visitors said Finnish government websites were experiencing a temporary disruption and were fully or partly unavailable while the issue was being resolved. That suggests the vulnerability has affected governments beyond Canada. The report by The Canadian Press was first published on Oct. 21, 2026, and included files from The Associated Press.

stories.Headline: Not Intel. Not CoreWeave. This Underappreciated Nvidia-Backed Company Is Growing Artificial Intelligence (AI) Revenue by 123%. Here's Why It's a Buy Today for $8.
stories.Summary:
Nokia, the Finnish telecom company best remembered for its early mobile phones, is being pitched as an underappreciated AI infrastructure play after its third-quarter earnings report. Motley Fool writer Adam Spatacco argued on October 23, 2026, that the company is using its network assets to supply AI networking equipment, with Nvidia as a key backer. Nvidia invested $1 billion in Nokia last October and took a 2.9% stake. The two companies are working on AI radio access networks, known as AI-RAN, which pair traditional wireless equipment with accelerated computing to turn telecom networks into distributed AI platforms.

Nokia's third-quarter revenue came in at 5.2 billion euros, up only 9% year over year on a constant-currency basis. Operating profit rose 35% to 605 million euros, and earnings per share climbed 50% to 0.09 euros. The standout was the AI and Cloud division, where revenue grew 123% to 631 million euros and order intake jumped 118%. Nokia won roughly 1.5 billion euros in new orders during the quarter. Spatacco said its acquisition of Infinera has strengthened its optical networking capabilities, and he named Alphabet, which is pursuing a 13 billion euro investment in Finland, along with Zayo and neocloud providers as companies Nokia works with.

The case for buying rests on the author's own view. Spatacco argues that hyperscaler spending on AI goes beyond GPUs and memory chips to include optical networking and connectivity gear, and that Nokia sits squarely in that supply chain. He cites Omdia data projecting that the AI-RAN market will exceed $200 billion by 2030, driven by edge AI uses such as autonomous vehicles, robotics and industrial automation. At a price-to-sales ratio of about 2.6, he calls the stock a compelling long-term holding, and the Nokia share price shown on the page was $8.10. He disclosed positions in Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft and Nvidia, and The Motley Fool's Stock Advisor team did not include Nokia in its latest list of 10 top stocks to buy.

For context, a separate Motley Fool article from October 21 described a rough stretch for chip stocks, with the Philadelphia Semiconductor index falling more than 11% in a week. It said a hot inflation reading and worries about CoreWeave's debt contributed to the selloff, and that Marvell Technology shares dropped nearly 17% over five days. That piece argued Marvell was the one AI chip stock to own heading into 2027, citing new memory and connectivity products shown at the Open Compute Project Global Summit and a target of $70 billion to $90 billion in revenue by fiscal 2031. It also noted that Nvidia bought $2 billion of Marvell preferred stock in March.

stories.Headline: Nvidia’s Jensen Huang joined on stage by robot ducks as he hails Europe’s AI potential
stories.Summary:
Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang took the stage at the company's GTC conference in Berlin on Wednesday, 21 October 2026, flanked by small duck-shaped robots as he argued that Europe's engineering skills give it an edge in physical AI and robotics. The event, held at the tent-shaped Tempodrom, capped a European tour that had already taken him through London, Paris, Stockholm and Dublin. The robots were Microducks, 25 cm tall two-legged machines from French startup Pollen Robotics, developed with Hugging Face. Huang asked them to roll over and perform somersaults, though three keeled over at his order to take a nap, one needed extra persuasion, and another faced the wrong way at the end of his speech. Environmental protesters also briefly interrupted the keynote before security removed them.

Nvidia used the event to announce several products and partnerships. It unveiled DSX POD, a reference design for factory-built, containerized AI data centers that combines seven liquid-cooled Vera Rubin compute racks with Spectrum-X networking. The company says deployment could fall from six months to as little as 14 days at a prepared site, with availability expected in early 2027, and Huang claimed that at 2 gigawatts the design could save 54 million litres of water a day. Huang also introduced Agile ONE SN, a humanoid robot reference platform from German startup Agile Robots built on Nvidia's Isaac GR00T technology and a Jetson Thor compute module, also scheduled for early 2027. Agile Robots chief executive Zhaopeng Chen told Reuters the firm plans to produce 1,000 to 2,000 small humanoids next year with Nvidia, with production due to start late this year.

Huang said that every company in Europe will become an AI company, and that no region matches Europe's precision and craft in mechatronics, electronics and mechanical systems. He said Europe, often left behind by the US and Asia in the AI race and without a home-grown player on the scale of Nvidia, Anthropic or OpenAI, must play a central role, and should produce AI rather than simply consume it. He also said Nvidia's Hyperion car system is being adopted by more vendors, and that European telecoms operators are deploying Nvidia-powered computing for AI-RAN. Nvidia says it has committed nearly $10 billion to Europe's technology ecosystem and has built an early lead in the processors and software that act as robotic brains, which gives it a commercial interest in European industry succeeding.

Forrester principal analyst Paul Miller said Huang positioned Nvidia as a supporter and enabler of Europe's sovereign tech ambitions, noting that the company made 14 investments in European startups during the current trip. He cautioned, however, that Nvidia is not a European firm, so anything with critical ongoing dependence on it or any other non-European company is unlikely to meet the purest definitions of European tech sovereignty. The Register noted that the DSX POD timeline leaves out the work of preparing power, connectivity and other site infrastructure first. The 14-day claim is therefore a best case, and both DSX POD and Agile ONE SN are not due to arrive until early 2027.

stories.Headline: Microsoft says China-linked hackers used AI penetration testing tool ARTEX to compromise ConnectWise as part of a campaign targeting hundreds of organizations (AJ Vicens/Reuters)
stories.Summary:
Microsoft said on Wednesday, October 21, 2026, that a China state-aligned hacking group it tracks as Storm-0940 was behind the recent supply chain compromise of the ConnectWise Cloud Backup application. The group used ARTEX, a Go-based agentic AI penetration testing framework, to speed up scanning and reconnaissance, password spraying and abuse of OAuth applications at downstream victims. ARTEX was made closed-source after it was abused in attacks on South Korean financial institutions. Microsoft said the actor ran the tool at "machine speed" to automate attacks on hundreds of organizations worldwide since September 2026.

The campaign reached a wide range of sectors, including aerospace and defense, automotive, chemicals, energy, financial services, government, legal, manufacturing, media, military, semiconductor, software, technology, and think tanks and non-profits. Between October 10 and 14, 2026, infrastructure at 144.172.64[.]99 ran an automated password-spray campaign against 327 accounts across eight organizations, aiming at Microsoft 365 and Exchange Online. Microsoft captured more than 151,000 failed logons in that window, peaking on October 11 at 2,900 failures per minute, for over 111,000 failures in a single day. Of the targeted accounts, 48 received more than 1,000 failures each, and Microsoft detected no successful sign-in, token issuance, Graph call or directory change during that stretch.

That changed on October 15, 2026, when the AI agents gained access to the identities of multiple ConnectWise cloud applications and began using them to authenticate into customer environments. Microsoft said this let the actor operate without an interactive user sign-in, because the applications had already been granted access. In the ConnectWise case, ARTEX was seen trying to sign in to more than 2,250 tenants at 2,900 attempts per minute, a pace that leaves defenders little time to detect and respond. Follow-on activity included reconnaissance, changes to application credentials and attempts to alter privileges that could allow wider or longer-lasting access.

Microsoft attributed the activity to Storm-0940, whose operations it first detailed in November 2024. At that time it described the group's use of a botnet called Quad7, also known as CovertNetwork-1658, for highly evasive password spray attacks, and assessed the group as active since at least 2021. The group is also said to exploit internet-facing applications for initial access, move through networks using compromised accounts, and keep access by adding credentials to existing OAuth applications in cloud environments to reach Microsoft 365 resources. Microsoft said a share of the ARTEX-driven attacks gave the actor privileged access to an organization's cloud infrastructure, with several cases where the time from first targeting to privileged access was under three hours.

stories.Headline: Amkor Technology stock jumps on Nvidia advanced packaging expansion
stories.Summary:
Shares of Amkor Technology rose 8% on Wednesday, October 21, 2026, after news that Nvidia plans to greatly expand its advanced packaging partnership with the semiconductor assembly firm into South Korea. Under the expanded agreement, the two companies aim to raise advanced packaging capacity in South Korea, with a goal of more than 300% growth in interposer wafer capacity by the end of 2028. The effort sits alongside Amkor's ongoing work on new manufacturing facilities in the country. Together, they are meant to support higher production volumes for Nvidia's current and next-generation AI platforms.

The Amkor deal is one piece of a wider push by Nvidia to scale manufacturing across several supply chain partners as demand for AI infrastructure surges. Nvidia is working with Amkor, IBIDEN, King Yuan Electronics (KYEC), Samsung Electro-Mechanics, Siliconware Precision Industries (SPIL) and Unimicron Technology to expand capacity in substrates, advanced packaging, testing and optical engines. Nvidia plans to raise substrate capacity for its products 2.5-fold over the next three years. Samsung Electro-Mechanics joins Nvidia's substrate supply chain immediately through its existing South Korean facilities, and output allocated to Nvidia is expected to make up a major share of its total package substrate capacity by 2028. Nvidia is also backing Unimicron's substrate expansion in Taiwan through a capacity reservation agreement, with new capacity starting in the second quarter of 2027 and reaching full scale by mid-2028.

Nvidia is providing a $1.1 billion capacity reservation advance to KYEC to fund new U.S. testing facilities and equipment, with a target of high-volume production by April 2027. SPIL plans to expand its Taiwanese manufacturing capacity for optical engines used in co-packaged optics, aiming for a 15-fold increase by mid-2027 and then doubling that capacity again by late 2028. The articles do not include comments from Amkor or Nvidia executives on the packaging expansion itself. The reporting comes from Investing.com, which attributed the stock move to the news of the expanded partnership.

The latest agreement follows earlier ties between the two companies. Headlines listed alongside the article point to a $1.5 billion Nvidia and Amkor packaging deal for U.S. chip packaging about two months ago, and a report that total Nvidia agreements with Amkor now reach $3 billion. Amkor shares reportedly surged 16% after that earlier deal. Separate reporting from the same page indicates the stock later fell sharply, though the articles give few details on that decline.

stories.Headline: Micron Technology Maps AI Memory Future With HBM, DRAM and NAND Roadmap
stories.Summary:
Micron Technology laid out its technology and product roadmap for the AI era during a webinar this week, covering next-generation DRAM, high-bandwidth memory, NAND and advanced packaging. Scott DeBoer, the company's president and chief technology and products officer, said AI is turning memory from a supporting part into a central limit on system performance, capacity and cost per token. He said Micron plans to advance memory, storage and compute together, with higher bandwidth, larger capacities, better power efficiency and closer work with customers. The company said its 1-gamma DRAM node is already in high-volume manufacturing and will underpin products launched over the next 12 months.

On the specifics, Micron expects its 1-delta DRAM node to reach volume production in the second half of 2027, aiming for a mid-20% improvement in bit density and tuning it for AI products such as HBM5, vertical HBM and vertical edge inference memory. HBM4 is in high-volume manufacturing, and Micron is developing both standard and custom HBM, with custom versions carrying customer-specific memory and logic intellectual property in the base die. Vertical HBM would place memory directly on top of processing units, mainly to boost bandwidth, while capacity will grow more slowly because of heat challenges. Future HBM base dies will use foundry nodes, and HBM4E will need more advanced CMOS than HBM4 did. LPDDR6 is expected to deliver 35% better power performance than LPDDR5, DDR6 is described as offering twice the bandwidth of DDR5, and a 1-terabyte RDIMM is planned after the recently sampled 512-gigabyte DDR5 RDIMM.

In NAND, Micron's Generation 11 technology will ramp in the second half of 2027, with more than 400 layers and wafer-on-wafer bonding. It is meant to more than double bit density compared with Generation 9, target 1.5 times the I/O speed and cut data-transfer energy. The company also described high-IOPS SLC-based designs for ultra-fast storage and high-bandwidth NAND that stacks NAND and logic dies closer to compute. Micron said it is using AI internally as well, citing a data center controller that went from silicon to tape-out in half the time of the prior generation and a data center SSD effort finished with 60% less time than before.

DeBoer was the main voice for the company, and he addressed several technical debates. He said capacitor pitch is the basic determinant of DRAM bit density and rejected the idea that 4F² architectures inherently beat 6F² designs, arguing that fundamental physics problems with scaling 4F² will ultimately bring in 3D DRAM instead. He said Micron is confident in several more generations of planar DRAM scaling before 3D DRAM arrives, with timing depending on cost, complexity and device performance. He added that the right NAND designs will be settled with customers, given differing needs across data center, automotive and edge uses.

For context, Micron pointed to longer-term investments, including expanded Micron Ventures activity, work at Albany NanoTech on advanced lithography and a previously announced $10 billion, 10-year commitment to Micron Research Labs. DeBoer said the company works with partners ranging from startup Liqid to Meta, and that Micron and Meta recently published a white paper on optimizing LPDDR6 for data centers. Asked about system design, he said memory setups will differ across training, inference, edge and rack-scale deployments, but more memory content and bandwidth consistently improve performance. He also said Micron does not expect memory supply to come into balance over the next two years, citing earlier comments from company leadership.
