stories.Headline: Singapore sets aside $45m to help advanced manufacturing SMEs use AI solutions
stories.Summary:
Singapore has set aside more than $45 million over the next three years to help small and medium-sized enterprises in advanced manufacturing deploy artificial intelligence solutions. Minister of State for Energy, Trade and Industry Gan Siow Huang announced the measure on Oct 21 at the Industrial Transformation Asia-Pacific event held at the Suntec Singapore Convention and Exhibition Centre. It is one of several initiatives under the country's national AI strategy. The funding supports a programme called Catalytic AI Solutions, which is meant to make the technology more affordable and easier to access for smaller firms.

Under the initiative, Enterprise Singapore will co-fund the adoption of AI solutions for eligible SMEs. The agency will work with trade associations, chambers and qualified vendors to offer a suite of ready-to-deploy tools for tasks such as optimising product and component design, improving production scheduling and carrying out predictive maintenance. According to Xinhua, the programme is aimed at barriers including high development costs, limited access to industry-specific solutions and uncertainty about outcomes. Enterprise Singapore also plans to extend similar support to the logistics and wholesale trade sectors, with more details to follow.

Gan said that AI should be available to smaller manufacturers as well as large ones, and that the initiative would help firms raise productivity and competitiveness. Wong Zeng Yi, assistant managing director for manufacturing at Enterprise Singapore, said AI could help manufacturers improve productivity, quality and responsiveness, and open new revenue through faster innovation. Gan also said that technologies such as robotics, digital twins and AI could strengthen Singapore's position as a global hub for advanced manufacturing. Separately, a manufacturing jobs portal developed by the Singapore Manufacturing Federation was announced, and Gan encouraged employers and job seekers to sign up for its Manufacturing and Talent Connection Hub, which is expected to open later in 2026.

The initiative sits within a wider push that Prime Minister Lawrence Wong announced at Budget 2026, which includes national AI missions in advanced manufacturing, connectivity, finance and healthcare, as well as a National AI Council that he chairs. The advanced manufacturing mission aims to grow the sector's output and productivity, and the AI Centre of Excellence for Manufacturing, set up by A*STAR and the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry in September 2024, is an important part of it. Gan said the centre has worked with 30 manufacturers across sectors including aerospace, semiconductors, pharmaceuticals and energy, and has completed 23 projects deploying AI solutions. The centre is now entering a new phase to tackle more complex problems and extend AI adoption to a broader range of manufacturers.

Articles.Title: Singapore sets aside $45m to help advanced manufacturing SMEs use AI solutions - The Straits Times
Singapore sets aside 35 mln USD to help advanced manufacturers adopt AI - Xinhua

stories.Headline: Websites go dark worldwide as AI uncovers flaws in code powering much of the internet
stories.Summary:
Governments and companies around the world took websites offline on Oct 22 as they rushed to guard against hacks, after artificial intelligence uncovered two critical flaws in PHP, a programming language that helps run about 70% of the world's websites, according to Wiz Research. The PHP Foundation, which maintains the language, released emergency security updates on Oct 21 for the two flaws, which are known collectively as PHP2Shell. The security firm Calif found the first flaw on Aug 1 using OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol model, during an OpenAI-funded audit of the language's code. Wiz, which is owned by Google, found its own flaw independently on Aug 19, using Google's Gemini 4 Argon, GPT-5.6 Sol and its own research agent. Details leaked online on Oct 20, a day before the planned fix, which set off the scramble to pull sites offline before hackers could act.

The flaws can let attackers into servers without a username or password, and both carry a severity rating of 9.2 out of 10. The US National Security Agency told organisations to patch immediately or take vulnerable systems offline, and authorities from Japan to the European Union said the same. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency urged updates to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35, and the FBI advised organisations to list every place PHP runs, including products that bundle it. Government sites in Australia, Finland, the Netherlands, France and Denmark went dark, while in Japan MUFG Bank halted some online transactions, Mizuho stopped services, Shizuoka Bank shut its banking app, and All Nippon Airways disabled boarding passes in Apple Wallet. The network that settles funds between almost all Japanese banks was not affected.

The Cyber Security Agency of Singapore said the flaws affect all versions of PHP and reported widespread exploitation attempts and several proof-of-concept exploits, though it knew of no Singapore sites taken down by hackers. The Government Technology Agency of Singapore said there was currently no sign any government systems had been compromised, and that some services might be taken offline temporarily as a precaution. The PHP Foundation said anyone running PHP must update now, and one of its security engineers, Volker Dusch, told the Wall Street Journal it was the most serious problem the language has faced in over a decade, comparable to the Heartbleed flaw of 2014. A Wiz blog post said the findings rank among the most severe ever found in PHP, and arguably in software history. OpenAI said the discovery marks a new phase in which AI can find security bugs with internet-scale impact, and it also warned that such tools can help attackers build exploits.

Only sites that run PHP on their own servers are exposed, and many large platforms use other languages or operators able to install the fix quickly, so they stayed online. Cybersecurity lecturer Rahat Masood of the University of New South Wales called the discovery quite devastating, saying attackers who get in can do almost anything, from stealing information to changing site content. Steve Kerrison of James Cook University's Singapore campus said larger institutions should patch quickly, but many smaller sites and user-run blogs may stay vulnerable for days, weeks or months and could be used to spread viruses or spam. So far there is little evidence of damaging attacks, though data breaches could later feed phishing campaigns. The number of software vulnerabilities found worldwide in 2026 is on track to roughly double the record total set in 2025, and Cloudflare has reported millions of exploit attempts since the disclosure.

Articles.Title: Websites go dark worldwide as AI uncovers flaws in code powering much of the internet - The Straits Times
AI uncovers massive flaw in web's foundational code

stories.Headline: AI: From Artificial Intelligence to Automated Impact – aviation enters the age of the agent
stories.Summary:
AI in aviation has moved past the stage of experimentation, and the question now is what happens when systems start to act rather than merely answer. A CAPA Premium Analysis published on 21 October 2026, and a parallel Routes item dated 23 October 2026, examine this shift using discussions from T2RL Engage in London in September 2026. The analysis argues that the significance of AI for airlines will be judged by its impact on decisions and workflows rather than by its intelligence. It also raises the possibility that the customer interacting with an airline may increasingly be an AI agent instead of a person. According to the analysis, the commercial relevance of this change is already emerging as technology providers build agents that can discover, compare, book and service travel.

Richard Clarke, chief executive of T2RL, said the AI story had shifted, noting that AI was almost absent from the conversation two years earlier but that the focus on executing transactions had grown quickly. The article distinguishes traditional analytical AI, generative AI and agentic AI, the last of which connects reasoning to action across several systems. It describes an airline disruption example in which an agent could identify alternatives, check eligibility, change a booking and notify the passenger, while stressing that human approval should remain where the risks justify it. Obstacles named include legacy technology, fragmented data, complex integration and the need for rigorous validation and governance. The analysis places particular weight on distribution.

Surain Adyanthaya of PROS is quoted as saying that AI agents are increasingly becoming the shopper, while many airline offer platforms were built for people rather than machines. If an offer is hard for a system to interpret, it may never enter the set of options an agent considers, whereas a clear and executable offer may be selected even without heavy conventional marketing. The article also asks who will own the customer when an agent makes the decision, warning that an airline could provide the transport while another party controls the interface where choices are made. It concludes that competitive advantage will depend on connecting AI to real decisions while keeping control of the customer relationship, the data and the authority to act. The articles do not give figures for adoption or revenue impact.

stories.Headline: Rogers, El-Sayed outline differing approaches to tariffs and AI during Detroit Economic Club forum
stories.Summary:
Michigan's two U.S. Senate nominees, Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, appeared separately at a forum hosted by the Detroit Economic Club on Tuesday, October 20, 2026. Each answered the same questions on policies affecting the state, including tariffs, artificial intelligence, education and health care. The event came just two weeks before the Nov. 3 general election, in a race that Cook Political Report currently rates a tossup. A recent debate between the two had turned contentious, leaving little room for calm policy discussion, and they were set to debate again the next evening.

On tariffs, both men said the tools could work if used carefully, though neither endorsed the way President Donald Trump has applied them. El-Sayed said Trump's approach has been chaotic and has hurt the auto industry and workers, and he compared it to giving a cancer patient too much chemotherapy at once. He proposed pairing tariffs with an industrial policy, including building a $25,000 electric vehicle with a 300-mile range over the next seven years, with subsidies for the first two years that would then be slowly withdrawn. Rogers, once a champion of the tariffs, said Trump should end those on Canada because they ignore how integrated the auto business is. He also credited tariffs with bringing vehicle production back, citing Silverados coming to the Orion plant, a multi-billion-dollar investment, and General Motors adding about 500,000 vehicles built in the United States.

On artificial intelligence, both candidates said stronger federal guardrails are needed, but their approaches differ. Rogers recalled being briefed, while chairing the House Intelligence Committee before leaving Congress in 2014, on an early AI-guided missile that appeared to make its own decisions in a test. He said he would support a national security framework already in the works, though he still needs to review its details, and he floated a narrow antitrust exemption so AI companies could cooperate on safety alone. El-Sayed, an AI skeptic, called for a pause in frontier research and said the technology could take 50% of white collar jobs over five to 10 years. He proposed an SEC or FDA-style regulatory agency, rebuilding leading AI firms as public interest corporations, democratically appointed leadership for at least 50% of their boards, and government ownership of about 50% of their value.

The Free Press reported that the candidates also agreed on the need to improve education and tackle a literacy crisis to strengthen Michigan's workforce. On health care, Rogers advocated price transparency, while El-Sayed supported a Medicare-for-All system. Although the two were not in the room together, El-Sayed took aim at Rogers's past record, saying Rogers had argued NAFTA would be good for Michigan in the long run, when in El-Sayed's view the state has hemorrhaged jobs under it. The forum gave each candidate room to answer more complex questions than the debate format allows.

stories.Headline: Reps. call on state Senate to pass bill to regulate use of AI in campaign advertisements
stories.Summary:
Pennsylvania state representatives are calling on the state Senate to pass House Bill 811, legislation that would regulate the use of artificial intelligence in campaign advertisements. The reporting, published October 21, 2026, says the House already voted unanimously to pass the bill in June. Samantha Sobel reported the story for WHP in Harrisburg, and the coverage appeared on several local station websites that day. The push comes as lawmakers say AI-generated political deepfakes have become more common in campaigns.

The bill would require disclosure whenever AI is used in campaign ads and would set guidelines for how the technology may be used in them. It would also let candidates bring civil actions against individuals or entities that publish AI-generated content without the required disclosures. Penalties under the bill could reach $50,000. Officials say the legislation is meant to protect voters from being misled by fabricated statements attributed to candidates.

The primary sponsor is Representative Khan, who said candidates are now putting words in their opponents' mouths that they never said. Khan described the bill as bipartisan and said it has passed the House for two legislative sessions without any action in the Republican-controlled Senate. Khan also pointed to recent AI-generated attack ads as evidence of why the bill matters, while saying candidates are free to criticize opponents. Khan urged the Senate to act, saying the technology is already out in the open.

The articles do not say whether the Senate has scheduled any vote on the bill or what its leadership has said about it. The coverage describes the proposal as an effort to address a growing problem in election advertising, but it does not describe any specific ad that led to the bill. The articles also do not say whether similar measures are under consideration in other states. What happens next depends on whether the Senate takes up House Bill 811 in a future session.

stories.Headline: Google Is Unlikely to Axe Ex-NPR Host’s AI Voice Use Lawsuit
stories.Summary:
A California state judge has signaled that she will let a lawsuit by former National Public Radio host David Greene against Google LLC move forward. In a tentative ruling, Judge Shella Dean overruled all four of Greene's claims that Google used his voice without permission in an artificial intelligence tool, which had been challenged through Google's demurrer. The judge said she was taking the matter under submission after a contested hearing in Santa Clara County Superior Court on Wednesday. The ruling indicates that the court found each cause of action also stated a claim based on appropriation of Greene's voice and identity.

The articles do not say what the final decision will be, and the full text beyond the tentative ruling is behind a paywall. Greene's complaint centers on the claim that an AI tool used his voice without his consent, which the court's tentative ruling appears to treat as a viable basis for relief. A demurrer is a request to dismiss a lawsuit on the grounds that, even if the facts alleged are true, the claims fail as a matter of law. By rejecting Google's demurrer, the judge would allow the case to proceed to further stages rather than ending it at the pleading stage.

The articles provide limited detail about the specific tool, how the voice was used, or the remedies Greene seeks. Readers are left without the complete reasoning behind the judge's conclusions. Google, as the defendant, filed the demurrer challenging Greene's claims, and the articles present the company's position only through that procedural filing. Judge Dean is the official who issued the tentative ruling and who must decide whether to finalize it.

The articles quote the judge's written language, stating that every cause of action states a claim based on appropriation of Greene's voice and identity and that a demurrer cannot be directed at those claims. Beyond that quoted passage, the articles do not describe further statements from Google or Greene's legal team. The dispute sits within a broader debate over whether voices and likenesses can be used in AI systems without permission, though the articles do not elaborate on that wider context. Whether the judge will issue a final ruling, and when, is not stated.

stories.Headline: Angelic Rountree: Conduct stress testing before deploying AI systems in law enforcement
stories.Summary:
Stress testing has become a critical step before law enforcement agencies deploy AI systems for forensic analysis, according to an article published on October 22, 2026 by Identity Week. The piece describes how the D.C. Department of Forensic Sciences tests AI biometric tools against real casework scenarios to find their limits and measure real-world error rates. The tests include degraded prints, mixed substrates, distorted images, and curved surfaces. The article does not give specific figures for error rates or test results. Angelic Browntree, Unit Manager at the D.C. Department of Forensic Sciences, is quoted describing the difficulties that remain in biometric work.

Separating close non-matches, which helps reduce false-identification errors, is hard for these systems. Matching a print against older database enrollments is also difficult because skin changes naturally over time. The article notes that deep learning tools in Automated Fingerprint Identification Systems have improved match probability by stabilizing ridge flows and filtering background noise. Browntree is reported to believe that AI and biometric technology will improve efficiency, serve as a triage layer, and speed up casework, with greater use of statistical models. She is also said to hold that human examiners will stay essential for the final decision because of the complex environmental variables involved in how latent prints are left behind.

The article presents these views as her assessment rather than as an agency policy. It does not describe any new rule, requirement, or legal change tied to these statements. The piece sits within Identity Week's broader coverage of biometrics and digital identity, which in the same period included other reports on identity regulation and law enforcement impersonation. The article does not say what steps, if any, the D.C. Department of Forensic Sciences or other agencies will take next.

Articles.Title: Angelic Rountree: Conduct stress testing before deploying AI systems in law enforcement - identityweek.net

stories.Headline: OpenClaw creator spent $10 million on AI tokens last month
stories.Summary:
Pete Steinberger, the creator of OpenClaw, an AI digital assistant, said he spent $10 million on AI tokens last month. He now works for OpenAI, and he made the disclosure during a conversation with Cloudflare CEO Dane Knecht at the Cloudflare Connect 2026 Conference in San Francisco. The article was published on October 23, 2026, and it draws on a report by The Register. The remarks were made in front of an audience of industry attendees, which the article suggests included people concerned about AI costs. The piece frames the figure as a sign of how quickly token spending can climb for users of the tool.

Knecht remarked that Steinberger had a virtually unlimited token budget, which not everyone in the room had. Steinberger responded that people do not always understand that not all of that spending is useful. He also questioned whether companies' infrastructure was adequate, asking why the tool still ran on his own computer when it could be in the cloud. The article notes that adding cloud costs and setting aside privacy concerns would not have reassured the audience. It describes the exchange as unlikely to calm chief financial officers already worried about the real cost of AI tokens.

The article attributes the spending and the remarks to Steinberger, who works for OpenAI. It presents his comments as paraphrased and quoted from the conference conversation, reported by The Register. Knecht's role was to raise the issue of the budget, and the article does not describe any response from OpenAI. The writer, Maxwell Cooter, notes that the spending may please Steinberger's employer as it prepares for an upcoming initial public offering. The article does not state any formal findings or regulatory action connected to the spending.

The broader context is the growing concern among businesses about how much AI usage costs and whether it is being introduced in the most effective way. The article mentions questions about whether there are better ways to manage those costs. It does not report any scheduled follow-up, further statements, or changes to OpenClaw's pricing. The available reporting is limited to the conference exchange and the figure Steinberger gave.

Articles.Title: OpenClaw creator spent $10 million on AI tokens last month

stories.Headline: Blackstone Pulls In $63 Billion in Third Quarter on AI, Energy Demand
stories.Summary:
Blackstone reported its third-quarter 2026 results on October 23, with inflows over the trailing 12 months exceeding $270 billion, the most in four years. The headline figure of $63 billion is the amount the firm pulled in during the quarter. The private wealth business drove much of this, with assets under management there rising 15% from a year earlier to $330 billion, an all-time high. Third-quarter sales in that unit totaled about $9 billion. The firm also launched the Blackstone Private Markets Fund, known as BXPM, a product for investors outside the U.S. that spreads money across several private-market strategies at once.

Insurance assets under management climbed 14% to more than $300 billion, and the dedicated insurance solutions unit now serves 40 clients, more than half of which expanded their relationship with Blackstone over the past year. Investment-grade private credit assets rose 24% to nearly $150 billion. In real estate, data centers and logistics led demand and together make up 54% of the firm's global real estate portfolio. Blackstone expects data center leasing to triple this year, while new supply across several property types has fallen to its lowest level in more than a decade and construction costs keep rising.

Blackstone justified its large investments by pointing to a shortage of infrastructure and capital relative to the fast growth of the artificial intelligence industry. Chairman Stephen Schwarzman said that AI and energy infrastructure are the core investment themes driving growth in the global economy and financial markets. The firm presented these figures as evidence that its strategy is working as demand for those assets accelerates. The articles do not say what comes next for these inflows or the new fund beyond the figures reported.

stories.Headline: Nvidia Shifts AI Data Centers to Factory-Built Pods to Speed Revenue
stories.Summary:
Nvidia has begun shifting artificial intelligence data center construction toward factory-built units, a change that could sharply shorten the time between spending on expensive hardware and earning revenue from it. The company unveiled the DSX POD at GTC Berlin 2026 in Germany, and reports on October 21, 2026 described it as a single container designed to hold seven server racks of Vera Rubin, Nvidia's next-generation AI computing system. The container is similar in size to a standard freight container and weighs about 28 metric tons. Cabling and liquid cooling piping are installed and tested at the factory before the unit is trucked to the site.

The design is also meant to improve power and cooling. Vera Rubin supports dry cooling, which releases heat into outside air, and the server racks receive 800-volt direct current power to reduce transmission losses. Because much of the installation work is completed in the factory, on-site labor is reduced, and Nvidia expects installation time to fall to as little as 14 days from six months. That estimate assumes supporting infrastructure is already in place and does not account for site preparation or grid connection. Nvidia also says the time between the arrival of computing equipment and the start of token production could drop to about one month from four to five months.

Seventeen global companies, including Dell Technologies, Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Foxconn, are working with Nvidia on the DSX POD. Nvidia supplies the standard design, while server makers and manufacturers build systems based on it. Nvidia plans to begin supplying the systems through its partners early next year, and pricing has not been disclosed. Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang argued in his keynote that the timing of a data center's start-up strongly affects profitability. He cited a 1-gigawatt facility costing about $50 billion, and said a three-month delay could mean losing $10 billion in revenue opportunity if annual revenue were $40 billion.

The technology industry reads the announcement as Nvidia extending beyond AI chips and rack-level sales into data center infrastructure as a whole. CNBC noted that Nvidia, once a semiconductor company, now supplies a range of products needed to run data centers, including networking and storage. Huang said the approach will transform the global supply chain and change how data centers are installed and built. The articles do not describe any further rollout timelines beyond the early-next-year supply plan.

Articles.Title: Nvidia Shifts AI Data Centers to Factory-Built Pods to Speed Revenue - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: AI Standing Orders in Ohio Federal Courts: Scope and Proof of Violations
stories.Summary:
Ohio federal judges have published standing orders that restrict the use of artificial intelligence in preparing court filings, and a commentary from the law firm Epstein Becker Green, dated October 23, 2026, examines what those orders cover and how a violation could be proven. Some orders ban AI use outright. In the Northern District of Ohio, Judge Christopher A. Boyko's standing order bars attorneys and self-represented parties from using AI in preparing any filing, while exempting information drawn from legal and internet search engines such as Westlaw, LexisNexis, Google, and Bing. District Judge Charles Esque Fleming takes a substantially similar approach, and potential sanctions under these orders include striking a pleading, monetary penalties, contempt, and dismissal.

The restrictions do not match one another. Magistrate Judge Jonathan D. Greenberg's order also bans generative AI in preparing filings and allows information from legal search engines, but it expressly prohibits Google and Bing AI Overviews, so a search allowed under the Boyko and Fleming orders could return output that Greenberg's order forbids. The orders also leave open whether AI used for summarizing testimony, suggesting arguments, proofreading, or other non-drafting work counts as "preparation." The authors note that the provisions do not separately address these uses or exempt work a lawyer later verifies. The orders require parties to notify the court immediately upon discovering AI use in a filed document, but they do not explain how disputed allegations should be resolved or require counsel to run detection software on opposing filings.

The authors say that counsel should not infer AI use from a brief's writing style or an incorrect citation, since neither proves AI use on its own. They cite National Institute of Standards and Technology reports noting that detection tools struggle with text that mixes human and AI writing and with AI-generated text that has been paraphrased. Even when AI use is confirmed, a violation depends on what the tool produced, how it was used, and what the applicable order permits, and a detector's score alone cannot establish those facts. The authors, Maurice Wells and James P. Flynn, advise litigation teams to check each assigned judge's requirements at the outset, communicate them to everyone contributing to filings, and document how supporting research was prepared. The article does not describe any specific enforcement action or pending dispute.

Articles.Title: AI Standing Orders in Ohio Federal Courts: Scope and Proof of Violations

stories.Headline: Malaysia's SkyeChip joins SoftBank-backed AI memory project in Japan
stories.Summary:
Malaysian chip designer SkyeChip has joined a SoftBank-backed effort to develop next-generation memory for artificial intelligence, according to a report from Nikkei Asia dated October 22, 2026. The company, based in Kuala Lumpur, will take a role in a Japanese semiconductor project that also involves Intel. The announcement was reported with a photo of SkyeChip founder and CEO Fong Swee Kiang, taken in Penang, Malaysia. The report frames the move as a push by the semiconductor designer into advanced technology as it expands beyond the United States and China. The articles give no figures for the investment, the size of SkyeChip's role, or the timeline for the project's output.

They do not say what specific memory products the effort targets or when they would reach the market. A related item in the same feed notes that SkyeChip targets Japan and joins the Rapidus ecosystem, which suggests the company's Japan activity extends beyond this single project. The available text does not confirm the full terms of that relationship. The report attributes the development to SkyeChip itself and to its founder and CEO, Fong Swee Kiang, though the excerpt does not include direct remarks from him on the project. SoftBank is named as the backer of the wider memory effort, and Intel is identified as another participant.

The articles do not say which company leads the project or how responsibilities are divided among the partners. The move comes as Asian chip designers look for growth outside their home markets, and the report describes SkyeChip's expansion as moving past its existing US and China ties. The articles do not describe any regulatory response or next steps beyond the joining itself. Further announcements about the project's scope, funding, or production plans would be needed to judge how the partnership develops.

stories.Headline: Why AI Requires CPAs to Look Beyond Traditional Risk Scores
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is spreading through business operations, but the controls around it often fail to show the full risk picture. According to an EY survey cited in the article, 98% of surveyed senior AI executives reported formal AI governance policies, yet 47% said their organizations had bypassed governance processes for urgent deployments. Another 36% reported an AI incident or failure with materially negative consequences, such as financial damage, operational disruption, or data loss. The article argues that a documented control shows only that a process was reviewed, not how a weakness could affect several areas at once.

Traditional risk assessments usually sort exposures into separate categories, such as cybersecurity under information technology, compliance under legal, and operational risk assessed on its own. The article notes that these categories are not sufficient when a single risk crosses their boundaries. Consider an AI tool that relies on inaccurate data, which can distort a financial forecast, expose sensitive information, and leave an automated decision impossible to explain. One weakness can therefore trigger several risk events, and assessing each separately hides how they interact and amplify one another. The article stresses that visibility into these connections matters more as AI becomes embedded across functions.

This shift matters because finance leaders are taking on more responsibility for technology decisions. Deloitte's September 2026 Finance Trends 2027 research, as the article reports it, found that 54% of surveyed finance leaders lead enterprise AI and technology capital-allocation decisions, and 48% oversee AI and technology spending and cost controls. The article contends that CPAs advising these organizations therefore cannot stop at identifying an isolated exposure. Their role includes helping clients understand how financial and nonfinancial risks connect, and how much warning exists before those risks become material.

Articles.Title: Why AI Requires CPAs to Look Beyond Traditional Risk Scores - CPA Practice Advisor

stories.Headline: CFOs Cite AI Cost-Governance Gaps in Survey
stories.Summary:
Deloitte released the third-quarter 2026 CFO Signals Survey, which polled 200 chief financial officers at North American organizations with annual revenues of at least US$1 billion each. The findings, reported on October 23, 2026, indicate that many organizations would benefit from greater real-time visibility, AI-specific controls, and rapid-response capabilities to manage AI spending once these technologies go live. The survey results were published as part of Deloitte's CFO Signals Series. They align with the Deloitte Finance Trends 2027 research, which anticipates greater cost and complexity through 2027. The central challenge for finance leaders is no longer simply deciding what to fund but building the cost governance and discipline needed to scale AI responsibly.

The article describes AI costs as volatile, difficult to forecast, and challenging to control as enterprises expand their use of the technology. Finance organizations may therefore need to sharpen their approaches to AI cost governance. The Trends report expects leaders to take on growing responsibility for AI trust, capital allocation, and cost management. Deloitte's findings suggest that finance functions must move beyond approving budgets toward active oversight of spending after deployment.

Nearly 80% of survey respondents said finance has a formal role in AI-related decisions within their organizations. Of those, 38% define or administer the evaluation framework, and 41% serve as required approvers. By contrast, 20% of respondents said finance provides only cost, budget, or accounting guidance without shaping the decision. The Finance Trends research found that more than two-thirds of leaders who oversee AI trust, capital allocation, or cost management assumed an owner or approver role within the past three years.

For many of these leaders, the responsibilities are relatively new. The article does not name a single party as responsible for the gaps; the findings come from Deloitte's survey and research. It notes that economic sentiment among respondents has also weakened significantly from the previous quarter. The article points readers to the full CFO Signals Series for further detail, and it does not report any planned follow-up actions.

Articles.Title: CFOs Cite AI Cost-Governance Gaps in Survey - CPA Practice Advisor

stories.Headline: Gov'ts scramble to patch websites after AI uncovers hidden PHP flaws
stories.Summary:
South Korea raised its private-sector cyber crisis alert from "attention" to "caution," the second of its four levels, on Thursday, October 22, 2026, after AI tools exposed serious security flaws in PHP, the programming language behind most of the world's websites. The Ministry of Science and ICT and the Korea Internet & Security Agency made the change one day after PHP developers disclosed two vulnerabilities. One flaw, dubbed PHP2Shell, could let attackers run code remotely without logging in and take over a website within seconds. Developers released emergency fixes, and the U.S. National Security Agency urged organizations to apply them and to take systems offline if updates were not immediately possible.

PHP powers roughly 70 percent of websites whose programming language can be identified, according to the web technology tracker W3Techs, including sites built on WordPress. Korea may be especially exposed because about 25,000 Korean servers ran PHP 8.1 or older, which accounted for 82 percent of those whose versions could be identified, according to the French firm CybelAngel. Those older versions no longer receive official updates, so users must move to PHP 8.3 or later to apply the new patches. Several European government bodies, including the French Interior Ministry and the Dutch National Cyber Security Centre, reportedly blocked access to some websites. Korean authorities have assigned more personnel to possible breaches and put emergency response teams on standby.

Song Ki-ho, third deputy national security adviser, warned that the scale of damage would depend on how quickly organizations acted and called for a unified response. Science Minister Bae Kyung-hoon urged a rapid response on Facebook, citing the risk of personal data breaches and website defacement, and advised organizations to check the PHP versions on all their systems. Organizations that could not update were told to block outside access or shut their sites temporarily. The flaws had been hidden in PHP's source code for years despite human review. Cybersecurity firm Calif used an OpenAI model during an OpenAI-supported audit in August and found them, after earlier researchers had judged them too complex for practical attacks.

Experts quoted in the reports expect AI to uncover such vulnerabilities faster and more often, and Yoon Doo-sik of eRoun&Company said open-source models could speed up both discovery and attempted exploitation. Some AI developers, including OpenAI and Anthropic, have delayed releasing their most advanced models over concerns about cyberattack misuse. Prof. Kim Seung-joo of Korea University said many companies do not fully know which servers they operate and called for a comprehensive inspection to prevent incidents. The articles do not say how many Korean sites have been compromised so far.

Articles.Title: Gov'ts scramble to patch websites after AI uncovers hidden PHP flaws

stories.Headline: Falconi US and Celonis Partner to Bring Process Data to Manufacturing and Energy Firms
stories.Summary:
Falconi US, a Chicago-based management consulting firm focused on manufacturing, has partnered with Celonis, an enterprise AI company, to help manufacturing and energy companies in the United States turn process data into business results. The partnership was announced on October 22, 2026, through a press release distributed by PRWeb. Under the arrangement, Falconi US consultants will work alongside Celonis teams on customer engagements in demand planning, inventory management and supply chain execution. The consultants will prioritize the opportunities the Celonis platform surfaces, design the operational changes needed to capture them, and support teams through implementation.

Bernardo Miranda, Senior Partner and US Managing Director of Falconi US, said that Celonis shows manufacturers where value is trapped in their processes. He added that Falconi US consultants have spent their careers optimizing those processes, so they can advise customers on which opportunities matter most and how to pursue them. Andrew Lieberman, Director of Partner Sales and Solution Engineering at Celonis, said that manufacturers' returns on AI investment depend on how well the technology understands how their plants and supply chains operate. He said Falconi US brings hands-on manufacturing experience that, combined with the platform's operational context, helps customers find and capture value faster. Both companies frame the partnership as a way to move from insight to measurable results.

The companies describe the Celonis platform as a way to build a real-time digital twin of operations by combining process data, business knowledge and information from connected systems, applications and devices. According to the release, the platform supports hindsight, insight and foresight, and provides tools to analyze, design and operate AI-driven processes across the enterprise AI lifecycle. The release notes that manufacturers already hold more operational data than ever but still find it difficult to turn that data into value. It also says that capturing identified value requires people who understand day-to-day operations and which improvements will pay off. Falconi US and Celonis say they are already working with customers, and interested manufacturers can contact Falconi US at the email address or website listed in the release.

Articles.Title: Falconi US Partners with Celonis to Help Manufacturers to redesign business operations with AI
