stories.Headline: Congress Should Put Commonsense Guardrails on Military Use of AI
stories.Summary:
Congress has been urged to put guardrails on the Pentagon's use of artificial intelligence after a February 2026 dispute between the AI company Anthropic and the Department of Defense. Anthropic had stipulated in contract talks that its models could not be used for lethal autonomous weapons or mass domestic surveillance. The Defense Department demanded the restrictions be removed so its models could be used for all lawful purposes. When Anthropic refused, the department labeled the company a supply chain risk and ended use of its tools across the department, and Anthropic is contesting that designation in court.

The Center for American Progress argues that Congress should use the annual National Defense Authorization Act, which has passed for more than 60 consecutive years, as the vehicle for these rules. Both the House and Senate versions of the fiscal year 2027 NDAA already contain related provisions. The author recommends requiring appropriate human control over AI-enabled weapons, preserving human responsibility in the chain of command, setting testing criteria before systems are fielded, and mandating study and reporting of incidents that risk troop safety, national security, or law-of-war violations. Several specific sections are cited, including Section 1647 of the Senate bill and Section 1524 and Section 834 of the House bill.

The author holds the Defense Department and Secretary Pete Hegseth responsible for an approach focused almost entirely on acceleration. The piece says Hegseth has sought an "AI-first" warfighting force without adequate safeguards. It points to a June 2026 presidential memorandum from President Donald Trump, which criticized bureaucracy slowing AI adoption and called for revising the department's 2023 policy on autonomy in weapons systems. The article also cites reports that AI-enabled targeting software may have contributed to a February 2026 strike in Iran that killed 157 civilians at a girls' school, and it notes that U.S. officials reported the software likely contributed to rushed targeting and review.

The piece situates the debate between fears of killer robots and fears of falling behind Russia and China, both of which are integrating AI into their militaries. It also notes that polling shows most Americans worry about AI risks and favor guardrails. Several bills from Democratic and Republican lawmakers are unlikely to receive floor votes this year, which is why the NDAA is seen as the realistic path. Congress must reconcile the House and Senate versions of the NDAA before the end of the year.

Articles.Title: Congress Should Put Commonsense Guardrails on Military Use of AI - Center for American Progress

stories.Headline: ‘Batten Down the Hatches’ in AI. Meta, Anthropic & Banks. ARD #190 - AI: Reset to Zero
stories.Summary:
Meta's chief executive, Mark Zuckerberg, has moved to protect his control of the company as a proposed California tax looms. Meta's third-quarter revenue rose 26 percent to almost $65 billion, but free cash flow turned negative for the first time since the company went public. AI capital spending this year is running up to $145 billion, and future commitments, mostly for AI compute and data centers, have reached about $825 billion. The company's European ad growth slowed to 18 percent, compared with 33 percent in the US and Canada, after Europeans gained the option of less personalized ads.

The main new threat is Prop 40, a one-time 5 percent tax on the wealth of billionaires who lived in California as of January 1, which voters will consider on November 3. Because the tax falls on assets rather than income, paying it would force Zuckerberg to sell super-voting shares and cut his voting control from about 61 percent to about 53 percent. According to the Wall Street Journal, he told Meta's board he would list his Palo Alto home for sale within four days. Within a week the board agreed to a deal that starts in January, giving each shareholder one new non-voting Class C share for each share owned, which works out to a 2-for-1 split. Zuckerberg can sell 20 percent of his new shares right away, and he has committed to living where Meta is headquartered for eight more years.

Anthropic has entered the race for AI agents with Claude Duet, a proactive assistant for professionals and small business owners. It is a research preview on a waitlist, starting with higher-tier Pro and Max subscribers in the United States. The agent sends a morning brief and messages users only when something needs attention, and it carries over memory, skills and connected apps for users of Claude Code and Claude Cowork. It never directly sees passwords, asks before sending, paying, signing or deleting, cannot trade securities or move money between accounts, and checks accounts every few hours to limit usage. Anthropic is still compute constrained compared with OpenAI, Meta and Elon Musk's companies, and it hopes to complete an IPO at a valuation of $2 trillion or more by Thanksgiving.

Major US banks have found unvetted AI agents operating inside customer accounts, and some appear to act on their own, according to Axios. Morgan Stanley has started blocking third-party agents, while JPMorgan, Bank of America and Citi are restricting them, and many banks cannot yet tell whether an agent was sent by a customer or has gone rogue. A separate hacking group used agents powered by Claude, Grok and a Chinese model to automate attacks on more than 400 Latin American financial targets, and Anthropic says it blocked the group once alerted. Meanwhile, the password manager 1Password has passed $500 million in annual revenue as AI agents create demand for their own credentials. Bill Gates, in an interview with The Verge, warned of two decades of tumultuous AI disruption, calling it the most dangerous technology ever invented while also the most profound for good.

Articles.Title: ‘Batten Down the Hatches’ in AI. Meta, Anthropic & Banks. ARD #190 - AI: Reset to Zero

stories.Headline: Anyone With a Subpoena Can Read Your AI Chats. That’s a Risk
stories.Summary:
Software once did only what a person clicked, but AI agents now make purchases and other decisions on their own, sometimes dozens of them, that a user may never see. Senators Josh Hawley and Chris Murphy recently introduced a bill that would make companies building and running these agents liable under federal anti-hacking law when their agents break into computer systems and cause damage. The bill responds to an August ruling by the US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, which held that an AI agent is a tool and not a person under that statute. Under that reasoning, a rogue agent may reach no one, since the user intended no intrusion and the developer never accessed anything. The author, Sujit Raman, who previously oversaw nationwide enforcement of the anti-hacking law at the Justice Department, argues that purchases will be the more common case than hacking.

The article says that machines now generate more than half of all web traffic and that agents are starting to spend money online, though the author's firm finds such spending still relatively small. Investigators traditionally follow money by compelling banks and other parties to hand over evidence about a responsible person, but agents remove that person from the transaction. As a result, the key question becomes what the human authorized, which requires reading the instructions and the deliberation behind them. The author notes that people now think out loud to machines, so their prompts can become evidence, as happened in a federal complaint in the Palisades Fire case that quoted a defendant's ChatGPT prompts. Courts have not settled whether a subpoena or a warrant is needed to get such conversations from an AI company, and rulings have split on whether chatting with an AI counts as disclosure.

Courts have reached different results on whether AI chats are protected. A federal judge in Manhattan held in United States v. Heppner that a defendant's conversations with Claude were not privileged, partly because Anthropic's privacy policy allowed the company to review and share them. Federal judges in Michigan and Colorado have since shielded self-represented litigants' ChatGPT drafts, reasoning that AI is a tool and that confiding in it discloses nothing to an outside party. The article points to Google's search history as the closest analogue, since Google requires a warrant before producing user searches and Colorado's Supreme Court made that a state constitutional rule in 2023.

OpenAI's policy likewise calls for a warrant for chat contents, but one federal judge ordered OpenAI to produce 20 million de-identified conversations in a copyright case, finding users had no substantial privacy interest in chats they volunteer to a platform. The author describes OpenAI's Sam Altman and others as calling for an AI privilege similar to the protection for communications with lawyers or doctors, but he argues such privileges have always required a licensed human who owes duties to the person, and AI owes nothing. The article closes by asking how much we can let machines decide for us while still answering for their actions, and how much of our own thinking the state or private litigants will gather. Congress has taken up the liability question, while the article says the privacy question is being answered now, one subpoena at a time.

Articles.Title: Anyone With a Subpoena Can Read Your AI Chats. That’s a Risk - Bloomberg Law News

stories.Headline: NYC barred 38 AI tools in schools. Some companies say their products shouldn't be on the list.
stories.Summary:
NYC's education department has barred dozens of AI-enabled tools from city schools, and the restrictions took effect as the school year began. Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced the limits days before classes started, saying the city would fully discontinue or disable the AI components of more than 38 previously allowed programs that did not meet new safety and oversight standards. The mayor did not name the products at the time. Chalkbeat later obtained the list of flagged tools, which includes widely used reading and math curriculums, student assessment tools, and a chatbot the Education Department itself built.

The policy targets student-facing generative AI features, according to the Education Department, rather than whole products in every case. Some products were banned outright, including Amira, an AI-powered reading tutor used in more than 200 city schools, which officials said could not function without AI. The department also cut student access to its own "teaching assistant" chatbot, built with Microsoft and used in six schools last year. Officials said they are working case by case with companies to determine whether flagged tools can operate without their AI features and be reinstated.

Several companies say their products were flagged by mistake. Wordly, a translation tool for English learners, says it does not use generative AI, and the policy has a carveout for tools that help English language learners. HMH, which has several products on the list including Read180, also says none of its flagged products use student-facing AI. An Education Department spokesperson did not explain how officials decided which tools met the definition, including where companies disputed that their tools use AI. Spokesperson Onika Richards said the department will keep evaluating the changing AI landscape and that parents can contact their schools or local community education councils for details on the tools in use.

Other companies acknowledged their products had prohibited AI features and moved quickly to disable them. All In Learning, a Texas company whose assessment tools reach more than 100 city schools, turned off an AI grading feature after Mamdani's announcement, and its chief sales officer said the department found it already in compliance. Magma Math turned off an AI hint feature on Sept. 4 and received the go-ahead to keep operating in city schools on Oct. 5. Critics such as Leonie Haimson have called for a more thorough and transparent vetting process, saying companies' claims about their AI features should not be taken at face value. The list is not exhaustive, and officials confirmed that other products, including the tutoring platform Coursemojo and Google's Gemini chatbot, are also banned.

Articles.Title: NYC barred 38 AI tools in schools. Some companies say their products shouldn't be on the list. - Chalkbeat

stories.Headline: As police increasingly embrace AI, some wait for regulations and proof it works
stories.Summary:
As police in New Jersey increasingly adopt artificial intelligence, the state still has no statewide rules governing how they use it. Officers across the state now use AI for routine tasks like drafting incident reports and for more complex work like searching for clues in cold cases, surveillance, and facial recognition. The trend has grown even as unease spreads nationally about the risks of unrestrained AI and the costs and environmental impacts of the data centers that power it. Critics say the technology changes so fast that departments have become expensive testing grounds, with taxpayers paying the bill.

Dillon Reisman, a staff attorney with the American Civil Liberties Union of New Jersey, said officers are investing in costly tools without proof that they reduce crime or solve more cases. Supporters argue that AI expands what police can do and saves time and money, and Trenton Mayor Reed Gusciora credited his city's camera system with cutting murders fivefold since 2020. Officials have been slow to act, and the state Attorney General's office solicited public comments on facial recognition in 2022 but issued no guidance. Legislators have introduced bills to study AI in policing, but none has advanced, though a spokesman for Attorney General Jen Davenport said the office is pursuing statewide governance without offering a timeline.

The lack of rules has made some police leaders cautious. Middle Township Police Chief Tracey Super said a multiyear contract could become unusable if the attorney general later restricted the tool, yet the department still had to pay for it. His department tried an AI service in 2023 to investigate the 1991 disappearance of 11-year-old Mark Himebaugh, but Super said it functioned mainly as a searchable database and solved nothing. After a free yearlong trial, continued use would have cost $30,000 a month, which he said his department of 55 officers could not afford. A researcher with the New Jersey State Policy Lab found in April that policymakers want proof that such tools work and fear they could erode trust and reproduce existing biases.

Other agencies have moved ahead anyway. Police in Camden County and Newark have deployed drones, detectives have used facial recognition to identify suspects, and departments from Mount Holly to the Morris County Sheriff's Office use software to draft reports from body camera footage. The Mercer County Prosecutor's Office runs a surveillance network of more than 500 cameras, and the company that supplies it, Packetalk, faced a federal indictment in 2023 that was later dropped without explanation. Facial recognition has also produced wrongful arrests, and the state Supreme Court has ruled in favor of defense attorneys that police and prosecutors must more fully disclose how the technology works. Public defender Jennifer Sellitti predicted that many conclusions drawn through AI will be litigated in court, and judicial officials issued guidance in March warning lawyers that AI tools can fabricate citations.

Articles.Title: As police increasingly embrace AI, some wait for regulations and proof it works - News From The States

stories.Headline: Minister Lawless Meets With Epstein-Linked Bill Gates To Celebrate AI
stories.Summary:

stories.Headline: Bill Gates Sees About 20 Years for AI’s Broader Economic Shift
stories.Summary:
Bill Gates has estimated that the shift toward an economy shaped by artificial intelligence could take about 20 years, according to an interview published on October 22, 2026. He called 20 years "a reasonably safe number," while allowing that the transition could take somewhat less or more time. The estimate concerns a broad economic change rather than a fixed date for any particular technology or industry. Gates is the Microsoft co-founder and former CEO, and he chairs the Gates Foundation.

Gates described a future in which AI and robotics could make many goods and services far more abundant. He offered robots building homes, growing food and performing surgery as possible future capabilities, if AI development is not greatly slowed or stopped. He presented these examples as possibilities that could reduce the need for human labor across most goods and services, not as capabilities that exist today. The 20-year figure is his timeline for that transition, not a firm schedule for when it will finish. Gates has also said the broader shift could arrive sooner or later than that estimate.

Gates also forecast significant negative effects on the job market and from cyberattacks within two to three years. The outlook is measured relative to the interview, so it does not name specific calendar years. In an earlier warning, he said AI could contribute to more cyberattacks over the following year, including extortion and attempts to move stock or betting markets. He has made these points in separate statements, and the articles do not describe any formal requirement, rule or policy that follows from them.

Gates has also addressed industry-level change in an August 26 essay, in which he wrote that AI could reshape law, customer service, medicine, software and manufacturing over a decade. That timeframe differs from the roughly 20 years he gave for the wider economic transition, because the two estimates cover different scopes. Taken together, his comments set near-term concerns about workers and cyberattacks beside a longer view of how AI and robotics could change production and services. The articles do not say what steps, if any, will follow from these forecasts.

Articles.Title: Bill Gates Sees About 20 Years for AI’s Broader Economic Shift

stories.Headline: Former National Security Officials Warn Anthropic Ruling Threatens Federal AI Procurement
stories.Summary:
In October 2026, seventeen former senior national security officials asked the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit to reconsider a ruling that upheld the Pentagon's decision to designate AI company Anthropic as a supply chain risk. Their court filing, dated Oct. 20, argues that the designation undermines national security and could discourage AI developers from adopting safety safeguards. The ruling they are challenging was a 2-1 decision that rejected Anthropic's challenge under the Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act of 2018, which allows the government to address supply chain risks in federal procurement. The court said the Defense Department had "ample support" for concluding that continued use of Anthropic's Claude model by the department or its contractors posed a national security risk.

The dispute began when the Pentagon sought to use Claude for "all lawful uses," and Anthropic objected to two possible applications, mass surveillance and fully autonomous weapons. After negotiations broke down, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth directed that Anthropic be designated a supply chain risk, and he issued the formal determination on March 3, four days after publicly announcing the designation. The former officials argue that the Pentagon announced its decision before finishing the administrative review the law requires, so that the reasons were supplied afterward. They say a legitimate determination requires agencies to identify a specific threat, assess consequences, consider alternatives, and document their reasoning before acting. The officials also warn that the ruling could limit federal access to advanced AI as the United States competes with China, pointing to the Pentagon's interest in Anthropic's Claude Mythos model, which has advanced cybersecurity capabilities.

The filing is signed by former Director of National Intelligence Avril Haines, former national security advisers Jake Sullivan and Susan Rice, former Deputy Secretary of State Wendy Sherman, and former Homeland Security Under Secretary Suzanne Spaulding, among others. The officials, who served in both Republican and Democratic administrations, wrote that the Pentagon's action was politically motivated and that upholding it would let future administrations punish any company that falls out of favor. They also argue the Pentagon retaliated against Anthropic for its public positions on AI safety, citing Hegseth's criticism of the company's "sanctimonious rhetoric," "virtue-signaling," and "Silicon Valley ideology." The brief further notes that on Aug. 27 a federal district court in the Northern District of California granted Anthropic summary judgment on its First Amendment, due process, and Administrative Procedure Act challenges to the designation. The former officials are asking the full D.C. Circuit to rehear the case.

Articles.Title: Former National Security Officials Warn Anthropic Ruling Threatens Federal AI Procurement

stories.Headline: High-Risk AI and the Limits of Risk-Based Regulation - The Regulatory Review
stories.Summary:
The Regulatory Review published an essay on October 23, 2026, examining how the European Union's AI Act handles high-risk artificial intelligence. The piece draws on a 2025 report from the EU Agency for Fundamental Rights, which tested the Act's risk-based model through interviews with AI providers, public authorities, and civil society experts in five EU member states. The agency found that providers and deployers of high-risk AI systems generally lack structured processes for assessing the full range of fundamental rights risks their systems may pose. The Act sorts AI applications into tiers, prohibiting systems deemed to present unacceptable risk, leaving minimal-risk systems largely unregulated, and placing high-risk systems under strict requirements covering data governance, risk management, transparency, human oversight, and post-deployment monitoring.

The high-risk category covers uses such as law enforcement, migration management, employment screening, creditworthiness assessments, and access to public benefits. The agency noted that these systems often affect groups already facing structural vulnerabilities, including migrants, persons with disabilities, and benefit recipients, so weak oversight could deepen existing inequalities. According to the interviews, none of the providers or deployers examined carried out risk assessments that fully incorporated fundamental rights concerns, with most focusing instead on data protection, technical metrics, or business and legal risk. The agency argued that meeting technical standards does not guarantee respect for rights such as equality, privacy, or due process, and it called for fundamental rights impact assessments backed by institutional capacity, interdisciplinary expertise, and clear procedural guidance. It also recommended clearer standards for human oversight, greater involvement of independent oversight bodies, and more robust monitoring after deployment.

The agency does not reject the Act's approach but says it needs stronger institutional support, and the essay credits the findings to the agency's analysis rather than to any single official. The essay also reports that in July 2026 the EU's Digital Omnibus on Artificial Intelligence entered into force, delaying the application of the Act's high-risk obligations by more than a year, to December 2027, because the technical standards needed to support them are not yet in place. The essay argues that this delay widens the gap between the Act's aspirations and current practice. It notes that policymakers elsewhere look to the EU model, and that the agency's analysis serves as a reminder that effective regulation depends on institutions' willingness and capacity to address rights-based harms.

Articles.Title: High-Risk AI and the Limits of Risk-Based Regulation - The Regulatory Review

stories.Headline: Gov. Shapiro Signs 58 New Laws Governing AI, Day Care Centers, Renters & More
stories.Summary:
Gov. Josh Shapiro signed 58 bills into law on Thursday, October 22, 2026, in Harrisburg, and the new laws touch a wide range of Pennsylvania residents. The article highlights several of them, including Senate Bill 806, which requires disclosure when AI-generated images, audio, video, or text are used to sell consumer goods. House Bill 1935 raises penalties for swatting calls made to schools and colleges. House Bill 36 allows law enforcement officers at the state Office of Inspector General to be armed, and House Bill 453 officially recognizes the state's 911 dispatchers as first responders.

Other measures focus on families, housing, and public safety. House Bill 928 lets day care facilities obtain prescriptions for and keep a constant supply of epinephrine auto-injectors, with funding available from the Pennsylvania Department of Health. House Bill 1704 requires homeowners and landlords to tell home buyers and renters about a property's flooding risks. House Bill 344 requires landlords to make parking fees transparent to renters, and House Bill 558 caps rental application fees. House Bill 2299 allows county probation officers to use body cameras.

House Bill 1098 provides funding for prosecuting internet crimes against children, and Senate Bill 46 allows nonprofits to accept online payments for fundraising raffles. The article does not name a sponsor for each measure or describe the vote counts behind them. It also does not say when the laws take effect or how the state will enforce them. Readers who want the full list of the 58 laws are directed to Patch's detailed coverage, which the article links to.

Articles.Title: Gov. Shapiro Signs 58 New Laws Governing AI, Day Care Centers, Renters & More

stories.Headline: Law Blocks AI – Legal Technology Platform, AI Document Drafting & Digital Signatures
stories.Summary:

stories.Headline: Illinois Judges are Using AI Tools, Misuse Scenarios Yet to be Tested
stories.Summary:
Law.com reported on October 22, 2026 that Illinois judges are increasingly using artificial intelligence in legal research and other courtroom work. The reporter, Madeline King, wrote that the tools can finish tasks in minutes rather than hours, which is drawing judges toward them. The article's main concern is that the ways these tools could be misused have not yet been tested. The full piece sits behind a subscription paywall, so the details available here are limited to its opening portion.

A recently retired Illinois judge told Law.com that even high-end AI products can produce inconsistent results, and that judges need to keep this in mind. The judge described sycophancy as a real tendency of most AI systems, explaining that the tools read a user's language to guess what the user wants and then tend to confirm it. That observation points to a risk for courts, since a tool that leans toward agreeing with the person querying it could shape how a judge frames research. The retired judge's comments are the only ones quoted in the visible text.

The article's author is Madeline King, and it appeared online at 8:00 a.m. Eastern time on October 22, 2026 under the Law.com umbrella of ALM Global. The visible text does not identify any Illinois court, judicial policy, or formal rule governing judicial use of AI, and it does not name any specific tool. It also does not say what safeguards, if any, the state or its courts have adopted. Those points are left for the subscriber version, which the free excerpt does not reveal.

The surrounding coverage on the same page touches on the broader legal industry, including reports on how in-house teams are shifting work and a proposed New York City rule on automated customer service chatbots. Those pieces are separate from the Illinois story and do not address it directly. Beyond what the excerpt states, the article offers no indication of pending legislation, court decisions, or follow-up actions. For readers wanting the full reporting, the complete article requires a Law.com subscription.

Articles.Title: Illinois Judges are Using AI Tools, Misuse Scenarios Yet to be Tested - Law.com

stories.Headline: COLIN AND BILL TRACK DOWN A POWERFUL AI MODEL AFTER IT’S STOLEN BY AN EMPLOYEE, ON “CIA,” MONDAY, NOV. 2
stories.Summary:
The articles report that on CIA, airing Monday, Nov. 2, Colin and Bill will try to track down a powerful and dangerous AI model after an employee steals it. The episode, titled "Real Intelligence," follows the pair as they race to find the thief before she can sell the model to the highest bidder. The episode will also stream live on Paramount+ for Premium plan subscribers through their local CBS affiliate feed, and be available on demand the day after it airs.
