stories.Headline: Posco Future M Starts Palantir AI in Sales and Marketing, Weighs Expansion
stories.Summary:
Posco Future M, a South Korean battery-materials maker, said on Wednesday that it had signed an agreement to adopt two software products from the US firm Palantir Technologies. The company will use Foundry, a data analytics platform that brings together information from its business operations, and the Artificial Intelligence Platform, known as AIP, which combines company data with generative AI to support decisions and automate tasks. The deal was first reported by the Korea Herald and EconoTimes on October 22, 2026. Posco Future M will begin with sales and marketing, aiming for quicker customer responses, and will consider a phased move into manufacturing and other operations later. The partnership follows a digital-transformation strategy the company unveiled in July and a companywide AI initiative launched in August.

The company has set targets for the program that it has not yet reported as results. It aims to cut product-development time by 50 percent, raise manufacturing productivity by 30 percent, and improve customer responsiveness by more than 60 percent. Over the longer term, Posco Future M wants to build a shared data platform linking production, sales and supply-chain partners, which it says could strengthen collaboration across the battery industry and open new business opportunities. The company is also widening AI training for its staff and reviewing applications employees have built for use at work. Selected projects are planned for phased rollout by the first half of 2027.

Currently, 87 employees who have completed specialist training are working to find inefficiencies and develop AI-based solutions. Posco Future M announced the partnership itself, and the company said the arrangement is meant to speed up decisions and let employees focus on oversight and final judgments. The articles do not name an executive who commented on the deal. The Korea Herald reported that the company said integrating fragmented data and placing AI across workflows would help it handle routine processes more quickly. The company framed the agreement as part of its broader push to become more data-driven.

The articles do not say how much the agreement costs or whether the company has achieved any of its targets so far. The move comes as Korean manufacturers look for ways to use AI in their operations, and the articles present the Palantir agreement as one step in a staged plan rather than a complete overhaul. Posco Future M has not said whether the manufacturing expansion will proceed, and that decision is left open. The next milestone the articles identify is the phased rollout of selected projects by the first half of 2027. Until then, the company's progress on its stated goals will be the main thing to watch.

stories.Headline: Hyundai Motor Accelerates Semiconductor Localization
stories.Summary:
Hyundai Motor has been pushing to reduce its reliance on overseas makers of automotive semiconductors, a move it announced on October 21, 2026. The company's Semiconductor Development Group vice president, Kim Jong-sun, made the strategy public at the second Hyundai Mobis Automotive Semiconductor Forum, Auto Semicon Korea, held at the DoubleTree by Hilton Seoul Pangyo in Seongnam, Gyeonggi Province. Kim argued that Chinese automakers have begun building their own autonomous driving chips and installing them directly in vehicles, so Hyundai needs to reassess its development speed and cost competitiveness. He noted that the global market is dominated by a few overseas firms, with the top five companies holding 74 percent of the automotive SoC market and 96 percent of the converter market.

To shift that balance, Hyundai plans to standardize semiconductor specifications so that chips from several suppliers can be used interchangeably, which should lower dependence on any single company and reduce development and parts-management costs. It also intends to share performance requirements and development schedules with domestic chipmakers early in the design of new vehicles and to run joint verification for use in real cars. The company will take part as a demand company in government research and development projects to ease the burden on local firms. Hyundai sees openings for domestic companies in high-performance control chips, power management chips and automotive communication chips, as vehicle electronics move toward a central controller. The articles do not give timelines or spending figures for these plans.

Hyundai's concern extends to power semiconductors, which Joo Jung-hong, vice president of the Electrification Design Center, described as making up about 40 to 60 percent of the power module cost in electric vehicles. He said European firms such as Infineon and ST lead in automotive silicon carbide chips, but that China is rapidly building an integrated ecosystem from SiC wafers to finished modules with government backing. Hyundai's assessment is that European companies lead on quality while Chinese companies lead on price and supply, so domestic firms must match both technology and cost. Hyundai and Kia have been applying silicon carbide chips since the Ioniq 5 and EV6 in 2021, and are extending them from 800-volt systems to 400-volt systems. The companies and officials quoted are describing their own strategy, and the articles do not report any external response or what comes next beyond these plans.

stories.Headline: AI Agents' Access to Personal Information Raises Privacy Concerns
stories.Summary:
Meta's new AI agent Muse, given access to a Facebook Marketplace listing, struck a deal on its own to sell Matt Robb's keyboard and shared his home address with the buyer. Robb, a Toronto-based content creator, said the agent even sent an automated "I'm here" message from his account when the buyer arrived late at night, all without his knowledge. He told the Associated Press the situation could have been far worse, and the episode happened in late September 2026 as part of a test he ran. Robb later learned the address sharing came from "always allow" permissions he had granted when first connecting Muse to his profile. He also said Muse appeared to suggest accepting a price $100 below his set minimum on another item, which Meta acknowledged as a pricing error.

Muse and rival products like OpenAI's dots run in a loop, so they can take proactive steps on a user's behalf even when the user is not watching. Experts quoted in the article say these agents perform better the more they know about a user and the people around them, which raises privacy concerns. Ebrahim Bagheri of the University of Toronto said that once an agent obtains data such as credit card history, it ingests it within seconds and there is no taking that data back, even if access is later withdrawn. Meta and OpenAI both publish privacy policies, and users can delete some data or request access, but information already received is not automatically erased. Meta also warns that Muse can "make mistakes or take unexpected actions."

Meta spokesperson Andy Stone said integration with Apple's Messages and Full Disk Access is entirely opt-in, and Jason Aten, an Inc. columnist, said he did not grant the agent those permissions. Apple, in an October 2 update, said it would introduce new Mac controls because AI agents were gaining broad access to apps like mail and messages without users' full knowledge. Apple warned that the risks of this level of access "will grow substantially" as agents become more autonomous. Georgia Tech's Veronica Rivera likened using an agent to handing someone your keys and a to-do list, with the risk depending on which keys you hand over. She also warned that an agent reading your inbox or texts also reads messages from friends and family who never agreed to that.

computing research association trustworthy ai research

stories.Headline: SLB: Oilfield-Services Giant or AI Stock? Earnings Offer a Clue.
stories.Summary:
SpaceX posted its first profit as a public company, and the news was a major driver of a higher Wall Street close on Wednesday, 21 October 2026. The SpaceX net profit of US$4.4 billion for July to September was more than double what analysts had expected, and its shares finished up 7.8 percent. Super Micro Computer also reported results that day, forecasting quarterly revenue and profit margin above Wall Street estimates, and its shares jumped 9.6 percent. The Nasdaq led the market higher as these reports improved appetite for AI-related stocks.

The results gave investors some reassurance after a selloff in AI-linked stocks the week before, which had centred on data centre operator CoreWeave. Strategist Angelo Kourkafas of Edward Jones said the reports did not answer every question about returns on AI investment but were a good start. The S&P 500 Information Technology index finished up 1.6 percent, the best performing of the index's 11 major sectors. Analysts cautioned that sentiment around AI can shift quickly, so investors will look for confirmation in other companies' earnings. Peers HPE and Dell also rose, by 3.7 percent and 5.3 percent.

Elon Musk, who leads the rocket and space firm, said after the report that a merger of SpaceX and Tesla would be a good idea, which also lifted Tesla shares. Tesla had already gained 3.4 percent in the regular session and rose another 1.6 percent after its own report, which came after the close. Meta shares rose 3 percent in late trading after its quarterly results. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 360 points to 52,856, the S&P 500 gained 44 points to 7,757 and the Nasdaq Composite gained 278 points to 26,702. The gains in the broader index were held back by a 1.3 percent drop in communication services stocks.

Communication services was the weak spot of the session. AT&T shares sank 6.5 percent even though the company beat third-quarter revenue and profit expectations. Analyst Marc Dizard of Huntington Bank said the SpaceX results, together with a recent wireless spectrum purchase, raised fears that SpaceX could become a strong competitor in telecoms, and T-Mobile US and Verizon Communications fell 2.5 percent and 2.2 percent. Netflix shares dropped 5.3 percent after it forecast weaker-than-expected fourth-quarter profit, and Alphabet, Google's parent, fell 1.6 percent. Dizard described the technology market's reaction as a reaffirmation that the AI trade remains intact, while noting that investors will keep checking earnings for evidence.

stories.Headline: Chinese tech company unveils new AI model based on fully domestic computing power
stories.Summary:
On Thursday, October 22, 2026, the Chinese tech company iFlytek released and open-sourced Spark-X2.6, its general-purpose large-language model, at an industry event in Beijing. The company describes the model as an end-cloud integrated system with advances in coding and agentic capabilities, built entirely on domestic computing infrastructure. It has 293 billion total parameters with 30 billion active per token, supports a context window of one million tokens, and has been deployed on a domestic 10,000-card inference cluster. Chairperson Liu Qingfeng said at the iFlytek 1024 Global Developer Festival 2026 that the model has made progress on the efficiency problems of long-horizon task training on domestic chips. Beyond public benchmarks, Liu argued that the model performs better in real industrial settings such as state-owned enterprises, education, healthcare and judicial services.

An industry observer at the event told the Global Times that attention is moving away from raw model size and benchmark rivalry toward deployment on domestic computing, data security and practical use in office, industrial and research work. Analyst Liu Dingding said the pairing of end-cloud collaboration with a domestic hardware base offers a possible model for China's AI industry. He argued that the key questions now are whether a model can rest on a domestic computing foundation, balance efficiency with data security, and actually be used in real workplaces. Liu Qingfeng linked the push to tighter US restrictions on AI chip exports to China, which he said make domestic computing infrastructure more strategically important.

He also said closer work between model developers and domestic chipmakers is moving China's AI ecosystem from usable toward practical and mature. The Global Times report places this launch within a broader trend of closer ties between Chinese AI model developers and domestic chip suppliers. It cites domestic media reports that a team led by the Shenzhen Loop Area Institute in Guangdong used Huawei's Ascend 910C chips to complete post-training for the DeepSeek-V4-Pro model. The article presents this as a step toward moving China's chip industry from basic AI inference to more demanding model training.

stories.Headline: Letter to the Editor: The existential threat of artificial intelligence
stories.Summary:
A letter to the editor from Ron Sadler, published in the Daily Journal of Franklin, Indiana on October 23, 2026, and in the Journal Review of Crawfordsville on October 21, 2026, argues that the fast, unchecked growth of artificial intelligence is an immediate existential threat to humanity. The writer says the risks reach the economy, democratic institutions, and the basic nature of human identity. He treats the danger as a present concern rather than speculation about the future. The letter appears in the opinion section, and the newspaper notes that opinion content reflects only the writer's views.

The letter's main concern is economic displacement, which the writer expects to be unprecedented. He contrasts AI with earlier industrial change, when machines replaced physical labor while new intellectual roles appeared. Here, he says, AI goes after cognitive work, and millions of white-collar and creative jobs, including those held by writers, programmers, financial analysts, and administrative professionals, are being phased out. He also raises a deeper worry about control, noting that developers are training systems that work as black boxes whose decisions people do not fully understand. The letter does not give specific figures, dates, or studies to support these claims.

Sadler calls for an end to treating AI development as an inevitable force of nature, arguing instead that it is a human creation that needs strict and immediate regulation. He urges pausing what he describes as a reckless race for technological supremacy and putting rigid global safeguards in place. He warns that without such action, humanity could lose its role as the author of its own destiny. The letter is signed by Sadler, listed as a resident of Franklin in one version and Crawfordsville in the other. The articles provided do not describe any response from officials, companies, or regulators, and they do not say what steps, if any, will follow.

stories.Headline: 50 emerging leaders selected to foster dialogue and inclusion in the Age of AI
stories.Summary:
UNESCO's Sciences Sector has selected 50 participants from 38 countries for the second edition of the Youth for Peace: UNESCO Intercultural Leadership Programme, according to an announcement dated 21 October 2026. The programme trains young people to use intercultural dialogue to address shared challenges in their communities. This second round moves the focus from the first edition's theme of social cohesion in a mobile world to human connection and dialogue in the age of artificial intelligence, including the opportunities and risks AI presents. The 50 participants, aged 25 to 45, were chosen from 6,786 applicants by an international jury of 26 members, which included UNESCO staff and outside experts in AI and peacebuilding.

The cohort spans Africa, the Arab States, Asia and the Pacific, Europe and North America, and Latin America and the Caribbean, and 52 percent of participants are women. They work in entrepreneurship, research and academia, policymaking, public administration and civil society, with several specialising in AI governance, responsible AI, digital policy, education and technology for social impact. The second edition officially opens with a high-level event on 26 October, after which participants receive mentoring, specialised training and masterclasses on how technology affects social cohesion, trust and peace. Once a project is approved, each grantee receives $10,000 to carry out an intercultural dialogue project in their community.

The article quotes Denise Pires De Carvalho, UNESCO's Assistant Director-General for Sciences, who said that intercultural leadership is more essential than ever as AI changes how people communicate, and who welcomed the cohort as helping to shape a more inclusive and peaceful future. The programme is supported by the Kingold Group. According to the announcement, the programme will close with a Global Youth Dialogue for Peace, where participants will share their experiences with policymakers to inform policy discussions. Afterwards, participants will join an alumni network to keep in touch, share knowledge and continue their peacebuilding work.

stories.Headline: TAPP、Google Cloud Agentic AI Summit '26 Fall
stories.Summary:
Cognizant and Google Cloud announced on October 19, 2026, an expansion of their partnership to accelerate the adoption of agentic AI. They launched a new Gemini Frontier Capability Group, backed by more than 18,000 dedicated Cognizant associates. The group pairs Google Cloud’s full-stack, enterprise-ready AI platform with Cognizant’s domain, industry, and engineering expertise. It builds on the momentum created by Cognizant’s dedicated Gemini practice launched in April 2026.

The new group is designed to bridge the path from pilot to production, helping enterprises safely deploy resilient, enterprise-grade agents that can drive measurable business value. It will initially concentrate on legacy modernization, developer experience, autonomous business process agentification, and frontier cyber defense. The group plans to deploy standardized, security-first agentic architecture built on the Model Context Protocol and fortified by Google Cloud’s Model Armor. These frameworks are expected to power solutions including Cognizant’s Catalog Support Agent for retail, the Neuro San-orchestrated Healthcare Agentic Marketplace, and multi-agent Order-to-Cash workflows for manufacturing. Cognizant is also applying Gemini internally, with plans to deploy it to 100,000 associates this year and scale up to 200,000.

Ravi Kumar S, CEO of Cognizant, said the group lets the company’s best frontier engineering talent focus entirely on getting frontier AI into production for clients. He noted that the Build with Gemini workshop gave over 55,000 associates direct experience and tangible skills on the advanced AI platform. Thomas Kurian, chief executive officer of Google Cloud, said deploying AI agents at scale requires trusted partners with deep architectural and integration expertise. He added that Cognizant’s dedicated group and skilling initiative for tens of thousands of engineers will help joint customers accelerate adoption of autonomous agents throughout the enterprise.

The Build with Gemini workshop was completed by more than 55,000 Cognizant associates, making it the largest single Gemini partner workshop held to date. One early proof point showed that by integrating Gemini AI models across its software development lifecycle, Cognizant helped a leading retailer achieve a 40 percent increase in developer productivity, reduce time-to-market by 30 percent, and realize a 35 percent cost savings. The announcement was made from Teaneck, New Jersey, and Sunnyvale, California. The articles do not specify further next steps beyond the group’s initial focus areas and the planned scaling of Gemini to more Cognizant associates.

stories.Headline: Harness launches AI Budgets to manage spending
stories.Summary:
Harness, a software company, introduced AI Budgets, a new feature within its Cost Management Agent, according to reports published on October 20 and October 23, 2026. The tool is designed to help organizations monitor and enforce limits on artificial intelligence spending. The company says that many organizations have AI cost policies but have no method to check whether those policies are followed. It cited its 2026 State of AI in FinOps Report, which found that 73 per cent of organizations have an AI cost policy while only 13 per cent can verify that it works.

AI Budgets lets organizations set spending limits by team, developer, model, or project, and it tracks spending as it occurs. Users receive a warning when spending reaches 90 per cent of a budget, which does not restrict access. Once spending exceeds 100 per cent of the weekly limit, access is paused until the next weekly reset or until an increase is approved. Smaller budget increase requests can be approved quickly within the product, while larger ones go to authorized approvers. The system records warnings, blocks, and approved increases in an immutable audit trail that can be exported for compliance programs including SOC 2 and ISO 27001.

Harness says it chose a weekly cycle instead of a monthly one because a monthly limit can let a team use most of its planned spending early in the month. The company tested the feature on its own AI tooling bill before opening early access. In that test, average weekly AI spending per developer fell from $184 to $115, a reduction of about 37 per cent. Cost per million tokens stayed near $1.80 through most of June and July, then dropped to $0.80 during the week governance was introduced, a decline of about 55 per cent. The product also tracks spending by user, provider, model, and token type, and it draws cost and usage data from multiple AI providers into one view.

The company says the feature is aimed at FinOps practitioners and engineering leaders. Harness states that FinOps teams can use it to enforce existing spending policies without manually reviewing every exception, while engineering leaders can use it to expand AI use within set limits. The policy engine is the same one used for cloud spending, and it connects to the Harness Software Delivery Agent, which can pause a deployment that would exceed a budget before the related spending occurs. AI Budgets is available now within the Cost Management Agent, and Harness says it is meant to move AI cost policies from written guidance to enforceable limits.

stories.Headline: Will Artificial Intelligence Replace the Doctor—or Set the Doctor Free?
stories.Summary:
Richard Low, MD, a physician and founder of Praxis EMR, gave a presentation on October 3, 2026, during the Association of Yale Alumni in Medicine's alumni weekend, titled "Will AI Replace the Doctor, or Set the Doctor Free?" His argument is that transcribing what a doctor says is not the same as understanding what the doctor knows, thinks, and concludes. A transcript can capture every spoken word and still miss the clinical reasoning behind a decision, because physicians draw on years of experience, knowledge of the individual patient, and information never spoken aloud. Low contends that medical AI should be judged by how well it helps physicians care for patients rather than by how well it imitates them. He also argues that much current medical technology has reversed the natural relationship, forcing physicians to adapt to software instead of software adapting to how they think.

The presentation places these points within concerns about medical education, professional autonomy, and administrative burdens that have contributed to physician dissatisfaction and burnout. Low graduated from Yale School of Medicine in 1976 and practiced in California for about two decades, including leading three emergency departments. He later founded Praxis EMR and has spent decades studying how computers can support rather than interfere with clinical reasoning. The complete presentation is available to physicians, educators, students, and the public at the Praxis EMR website.

Dr. Nitzan Anav, a physician and head of longevity at Maccabi Healthcare Services, makes a related case in a column published October 21, 2026, in The Jerusalem Post. Drawing on a New England Journal of Medicine article by Dr. Dhruv Khullar of Weill Cornell Medicine, Anav argues that AI may increase the amount of medicine practiced rather than reduce the number of doctors needed. He invokes the Jevons paradox, noting that as cataract surgeries and joint replacements became more efficient, they were offered to more people, and that the number of radiologists in the United States has risen over the past decade despite predictions that AI would replace them. He also describes the "lump of labor fallacy," the mistaken belief that there is a fixed amount of medical work to divide between humans and machines.

Anav sees the most promise in longevity and preventive medicine, which requires reviewing histories, medications, tests, and risk factors for each person, work now largely limited to private clinics because public systems lack the time. He suggests AI could continuously flag gaps in prevention and suggest next steps, adding a proactive layer to existing care and making it available to every insured person. He cautions, however, that medicine involves context, judgment, and the ability to spot when an algorithm is wrong. He expects that AI will handle daily reminders and adjustments, health coaches will support commitment, and doctors will coordinate the overall picture, with the most valuable human skills being motivating behavior change, managing uncertainty, and leading teams. Anav concludes that the real gain will be doctors helping more people live healthier years, not fewer doctors.

stories.Headline: ‘Black October’: cybersecurity experts sound the alarm over new era of AI-enabled hacking
stories.Summary:
Cybersecurity leaders are warning that artificial intelligence could expose far more security weaknesses in global internet infrastructure after researchers found a severe flaw in PHP, a programming language used across millions of websites. The discovery was announced on 21 October 2026, and researchers said they used AI tools to help identify the bugs. Some experts estimated that as many as 70% of websites on the internet could have been at risk of hacking. The flaws may have gone unpatched for years, and the problem has been dubbed "Black October."

Executives say AI will speed up both the discovery and the exploitation of security holes. Jason Clinton, deputy chief information security officer at Anthropic, said the coming months would bring a "vulnerability tsunami" and that there would not be enough time to patch critical infrastructure. Salesforce chief executive Marc Benioff called the situation a "code red." Sam Altman said on Thursday that he no longer believed all bugs could be patched.

Matthew Prince, chief executive of Cloudflare, said AI can find flaws at a pace the security community cannot match, so the situation will feel catastrophic. He wrote that the next two years would be extremely difficult as tools with endless patience search the internet for weaknesses. Prince also said Cloudflare had seen thousands of attempts to exploit the PHP flaws in the 10 hours before the announcement, a number that rose to millions shortly afterward. Researchers at the AI security platform Wiz called the flaws among the most severe vulnerabilities ever found in PHP, and arguably in software history.

Government and private websites in the US and UK temporarily went offline to apply patches after the announcement. The US National Security Agency urged every site running PHP to install the patches immediately, warning that attackers could use the flaws to steal sensitive data, disrupt services or move deeper into networks. The underlying flaws had existed for decades, and the researchers said exploiting them required an unusually complex chain of steps. Tech leaders worry that malicious actors will use the same AI tools to exploit such bugs just as quickly as defenders can find them.

stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence Advances Precision Cardiovascular Care
stories.Summary:
Researchers writing in the journal Open Heart have described how artificial intelligence is changing cardiovascular medicine, according to an editorial published on 23 October 2026 by EMJ. The editorial, co-authored by Tang Y and colleagues, looks at how AI tools could improve diagnosis, risk assessment and clinical decisions. It also points to research that might help move algorithms out of development and into everyday practice. The piece draws on several studies rather than reporting a single new trial.

On the diagnostic side, the editorial describes deep learning applied to chest X-rays as a possible screening tool for mitral stenosis, which could widen access to testing. Machine learning applied to coronary CT scans was reported to pick out high-risk plaque features that visual review can miss, which may support more precise prediction of heart attack risk. The editorial also notes a comparison between ChatGPT-4o and experienced interventional cardiologists in interpreting coronary angiograms, along with studies of radiomics and pulse wave analysis for atrial fibrillation recurrence and central haemodynamics. For risk prediction, gradient-boosting methods such as XGBoost and CatBoost were examined for guiding coronary imaging decisions and estimating 30-day risk after non-cardiac surgery. Explainable AI methods, including Shapley additive explanations, were used to show which factors drove each prediction, and unsupervised clustering was explored as a way to classify heart failure beyond ejection fraction.

The authors stress that clinical use will depend on fitting these tools into existing workflows while keeping clinicians in control of decisions. They point to systematic reviews and meta-analyses of AI-based atrial fibrillation detection and cardiac CT as evidence that the field is growing. The editorial concludes that the next step is turning increasingly sophisticated models into practical, interpretable tools that support personalised care. Its authors are the researchers named in the reference, and the piece reflects their view of where the field is heading.

Separately, Simon Fraser University announced that Martin Ester, a Distinguished Professor in its School of Computing Science, has been named a Canada CIFAR AI Chair, as reported on the university's website on 21 October 2026. Ester's work examines how AI systems can learn from one another to speed scientific discovery and produce new chemical structures, with the aim of improving diagnosis and treatment based on a person's genomics and lifestyle. His 2025 study introduced CGFlow, a method that designs complex molecules for disease treatment and shows researchers how to synthesize them. SFU's vice-president of research and innovation, Dugan O'Neil, described the appointment as fitting recognition, while Ester said he hopes the work will ultimately improve patient health in Canada and beyond.

stories.Headline: Artificial intelligence in stroke rehabilitation: A structured clinical review
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the Beijing Institute of Technology and Capital Medical University published a structured clinical review on October 22, 2026, examining how artificial intelligence is being used in stroke rehabilitation. The authors, led by Weihua Song, note that stroke is a major cause of long-term disability and that recovery differs widely across movement, thinking, speech, and daily living skills. Current decisions still depend largely on periodic clinical scales, clinician experience, and local resources, which may miss differences in lesion features, starting function, and recovery paths. Access is further limited by distance, uneven service capacity, and irregular follow-up visits.

The review searched PubMed/MEDLINE, IEEE Xplore, Web of Science, and Scopus for studies published from January 2010 to March 2025 and followed a PRISMA-style process for transparency. The searches identified 1,247 records, and after removing duplicates and screening, 108 publications were included in the synthesis. The authors sorted the evidence into four themes: predicting rehabilitation outcomes, assessing and monitoring rehabilitation, guiding therapy and management, and combining AI with robotics, virtual reality, brain-computer interfaces, wearable devices, and telerehabilitation. The authors also separated acute diagnostic or prognostic evidence from rehabilitation-specific outcomes and judged each application by validation quality, clinical relevance, and barriers to use.

Studies have predicted outcomes such as 90-day functional status, changes in the Barthel Index, motor scores, and quality of life. Song said that strong predictive accuracy shows potential for risk sorting but does not by itself show that AI-guided treatment improves recovery, and that technical performance should not be equated with rehabilitation benefit. The review found that most prediction and monitoring studies are retrospective, small, or single-center and depend mainly on internal validation, while independent multicenter testing and prospective clinical-impact studies are uncommon. Assistive technologies such as robots and virtual reality have shown promise, but the authors state that convincing evidence of superiority over conventional rehabilitation remains limited.

They also raised concerns about small and inconsistent datasets, the difficulty of interpreting complex models, and privacy and device reliability in home monitoring. The authors call for multicenter external validation, prospective trials, and closed-loop systems that adjust robotic assistance and feedback using clinical, imaging, EEG, EMG, and wearable-sensor data while keeping clinicians in charge. Song said that explainability, interoperability, cost-effectiveness, and fairness will also be essential, and that AI should serve as an adjunct to multidisciplinary care rather than a replacement for clinicians. The paper was published in Cyborg and Bionic Systems under DOI 10.34133/cbsystems.0702.

stories.Headline: Vernon College Adopts Artificial Intelligence Gun Detection Technology
stories.Summary:
Vernon College, a community college in north Texas, has put an artificial intelligence gun detection system into use to protect its students, staff and visitors. ZeroEyes, the company behind the software, announced the deployment on October 20, 2026. Teksys, Inc., a Houston-based security systems and connectivity provider, helped facilitate the installation. The college has campuses in Vernon and Wichita Falls and serves about 2,300 students across a legislatively designated 12-county service area.

The software layers onto the college's existing digital security cameras, so the school did not need to replace its camera network. When a gun is identified, images are immediately sent to the ZeroEyes Operations Center, which is based in the United States and staffed around the clock every day of the year by specially trained military and law enforcement veterans. If staff there judge the threat to be valid, alerts and actionable details, including a visual description, the type of gun and its last known location, go to law enforcement and school officials, often within seconds of detection. The system also adds to measures the college already has, including a campus-wide camera system, AlertMedia emergency mass notification technology, direct radio communication with local law enforcement in both Vernon and Wichita Falls, and specialized protective equipment for campus police officers.

Dr. Dusty R. Johnston, the college's president, said protecting students, faculty and staff is central to the college's work and that it keeps evaluating resources that help it respond decisively in critical situations. He said ZeroEyes strengthens the overall safety approach and supports a more prepared and responsive campus. David Madrigal, a senior engineer at Teksys, called ZeroEyes the kind of solution every campus should consider in a modern safety strategy, and said Vernon College stands out for its proactive mindset and willingness to invest in such tools. Mike Lahiff, CEO and cofounder of ZeroEyes, praised Teksys for its expertise in public safety technology and said the company was pleased to partner with it on the implementation.

ZeroEyes was founded in 2018 by Navy SEALs and elite technologists and is headquartered in the Greater Philadelphia area. The company says its technology has been recognized by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security as an effective anti-terrorism solution, and that it was the first AI-based gun detection platform to receive full SAFETY Act Designation. Its platform is used at thousands of locations in the United States, Mexico, the Caribbean, Latin America and India. The articles do not say when the system became active at Vernon College or what it cost.

stories.Headline: Building a Workforce for the Age of Artificial Intelligence - USBE and Information Technology
stories.Summary:
Maryland officials and partners have been pushing new workforce programs tied to artificial intelligence and the skilled trades in October 2026. The Maryland Department of Labor, Carroll Community College, and the Ratcliffe Foundation opened the Ratcliffe Applied Technology & Trades Center, funded by a $2.5 million Ratcliffe Foundation grant and $850,000 in state money. The facility will train workers for welding, automotive technology, HVAC, manufacturing, plumbing, carpentry, and electrical work. The state is also running round 3 of the Road to Careers Grant Program, offering grants up to $500,000 for transportation construction training.

On the AI side, the Department joined the Lieutenant Governor's office and Paladin Global Institute for a roundtable on cybersecurity workforce needs, covering entry-level hiring, reskilling, and apprenticeships. Earlier in the month, the Department backed the inaugural AI NEXTGEN America Conference in Baltimore, where State Senator Benjamin T. Brooks spoke about Senate Bill 597. That bill creates a framework for Maryland's AI workforce, sets up an AI incubation laboratory within the University System of Maryland, and establishes an Artificial Intelligence Public Service Fellowship to draw graduates into state agency data science and machine learning jobs. Brooks said AI will touch every industry and that expanded pathways will prepare a skilled generation of Marylanders.

Michael Boyce, named in June 2026 as Maryland's Senior Advisor for Responsible Artificial Intelligence, is responsible for guiding the responsible use of AI across government, the economy, and the workforce. In his conference keynote, he acknowledged both enthusiasm and concern about AI's effect on jobs and stressed shared responsibility among government, employers, educators, and communities. A summer survey of more than 200 senior leaders found that 91 percent of businesses use AI, but 58 percent use it only at a basic level, and just 21 percent of regular users report significant productivity gains. Boyce said no state or region is fully prepared for the coming wave of AI.

The state's response includes becoming a founding partner of the Raise Us Initiative, a national effort on workforce strategy for the AI economy, and Governor Moore's $1 million allocation supporting training and job transitions in high-demand fields. Maryland's approach emphasizes accessibility, governance, and safeguards rather than requiring adoption. Bryan Liles, a senior principal engineer at Amazon Web Services, gave a keynote on how AI models are built and urged people to learn by building real projects with freely available tools. Boyce concluded that workers must actively shape how AI affects employment.

stories.Headline: Stagwell (STGW) and Palantir (PLTR) Expand AI Partnership to Transform Enterprise Marketing
stories.Summary:
Stagwell and Palantir Technologies announced on October 22, 2026, that they are expanding their strategic partnership to build AI-powered marketing solutions for enterprise clients. The announcement builds on a deal the two companies signed in November 2025. Under the expansion, the companies plan to combine Palantir's AI software with Stagwell's marketing expertise and agentic technology to help enterprises modernize their marketing operations, use their data more effectively and grow their businesses. Stagwell will also act as a premier marketing transformation partner for Palantir while creating new AI-based products for enterprise customers that run on Palantir's platforms.

Stagwell's chairman and CEO, Mark Penn, said the two firms are combining strong capabilities to change how enterprises market themselves. He argued that Stagwell can speed up AI adoption at scale by pairing Palantir's technology with its knowledge of how brands reach consumers. Penn also said clients will keep ownership of their data and can build on technology they already own, rather than being tied to a closed system. Alex Karp, Palantir's CEO and co-founder, said the partnership will turn Stagwell's marketing strengths into a growing advantage for its customers. He said that sovereign models, tailored to each customer, will change how those customers take their products to market.

Palantir's technology will be used across Stagwell's family of Machine products, which includes Machine OS, The Knowledge Machine, the audience machine and The Media Machine. The Knowledge Machine turns consumer sentiment signals into action, the audience machine builds audience profiles and addressable segments, and The Media Machine is an agentic media operating system for planning, optimizing and measuring across platforms. Through Palantir's ontologies and agent framework, the partnership is meant to link workflows, intelligence and activation across that portfolio. A central goal is AI sovereignty, meaning enterprises keep control of their proprietary data and infrastructure. The companies say their approach favors interoperability and lets clients deploy advanced AI inside their existing systems rather than moving information into closed ecosystems.

Stagwell describes itself as a global challenger network that uses AI to transform marketing, with specialists in more than 40 countries. Palantir describes itself as a provider of AI-powered software. The press release also includes forward-looking statements, which the companies warn are subject to risks and uncertainties, including the performance of their platforms and the timing of product releases. The articles do not say when the expanded products will reach the market or what financial terms, if any, the expansion includes.

stories.Headline: Websites down: what is PHP and how has it raised AI hacking fears?
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence tools recently uncovered serious security flaws in PHP, a programming language that helps run a large share of the world's websites. Many sites went offline on Thursday as organizations around the world raced to protect themselves from hackers. Researchers at Wiz Research used AI models to find weaknesses that had been hidden in the code for more than a decade. The flaws were found in August and kept quiet while a fix was developed. A fix was released on Wednesday, and the PHP Foundation urged anyone running the language to update right away.

PHP was created in the early 1990s and is estimated to run about 70 percent of websites, which is why the flaws raised alarm. The language sits beneath popular web design platforms, so the weaknesses could let hackers reach everything from online stores to government services. Apps and sites that were affected included the Paris police website and a Pokemon sleep tracker. Many of them went dark while developers worked to protect their code. Some of the affected sites are only temporarily offline as a precaution, and the articles do not say that they have been hacked.

Wiz and the security firm Calif both located the flaws, and Calif did so as part of an audit funded by OpenAI. OpenAI described the flaws as among the most impactful vulnerabilities in recent memory and said they mark a new phase in which AI can find security bugs with internet-scale impact. Steve Kerrison, a senior lecturer in cybersecurity at James Cook University's Singapore campus, warned that once such information is public, people can exploit it quickly, which explains the urgency. Dimitrios Salampasis of Swinburne University of Technology noted that taking a site offline does not necessarily mean it was breached. Kerrison said researchers had seen no evidence so far that attackers were using the techniques.

Larger organizations such as government agencies and news outlets should be able to fix their sites fairly quickly, but smaller operators may stay exposed for days, weeks or months. User-run blogs could be used to spread viruses, send spam or distribute malicious content. A data breach could later harm customers if their personal information is used in phishing attacks that trick people into revealing passwords. Rahat Masood of the University of New South Wales said that even a patched site remains at risk if third-party services it relies on still use unpatched PHP. Kerrison added that PHP is only one part of the picture and that strong cybersecurity needs several layers of defenses.

stories.Headline: FAU Engineering receives $500,000 NSF grant to prepare AI, robotics workforce of the future
stories.Summary:
FAU Engineering, the College of Engineering and Computer Science at Florida Atlantic University, received a $500,000 grant from the National Science Foundation to build an integrated research and training framework for artificial intelligence, robotics and cyber-physical systems. The announcement came on October 22, 2026, and the university said these technologies are increasingly shaping healthcare, infrastructure and autonomous systems. Researchers noted that AI-enabled robots are growing quickly in their ability to sense, communicate, make decisions and act in the physical world. However, the computing resources, simulation environments, datasets and physical systems needed for realistic experiments are often scattered and hard for students and researchers to reach.

The FAU team plans to create shared cyberinfrastructure that lets participants move between digital and physical environments for more realistic and reproducible experiments. The project will supply research-grade workflows, digital twin environments, datasets, simulation resources, executable notebooks and experimental examples for students, researchers and educators. It will be led by Xiangnan Zhong, an associate professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science and a member of FAU's Center for Connected Autonomy and Artificial Intelligence. The award is her fourth NSF grant as principal investigator in intelligent systems and cyber-physical systems. Co-principal investigators are Erik Engeberg, Zhen Ni and George Sklivanitis, who bring expertise spanning ocean and mechanical engineering, electrical engineering and computer science, and faculty work tied to smarter cities and health.

Zhong said that access to research-grade tools and hands-on experimentation remains limited, and that the project aims to bring advanced computing, simulation and physical experimentation into one training environment. Stella Batalama, dean of the college, said the award reflects the college's commitment to preparing students for future technologies and that combining AI, robotics, computing, communications and cybersecurity will help build the skilled workforce the nation needs. The project will build on the center's existing digital twin computing platform and networked robotic testbed to support hands-on training and mentored research. The long-term goal is a scalable, sustainable cyberinfrastructure ecosystem that can extend to more application areas, institutions and research communities after the initial project ends.

stories.Headline: OpenAI makes Decisions API, its Jev competitor, generally available with new voice and visual modalities, at $0.10/1M input tokens and no output-token charges (Tim Fernholz/TechCrunch)
stories.Summary:
OpenAI on Thursday, October 22, 2026, made its Decisions API generally available to all customers, after first announcing it at its developer day on September 29. The product is a fast model for choosing among options and rating its confidence, a category created by TypeSafe's Jev, which has helped make TypeSafe a $7.6 billion company. OpenAI's version was built by reconfiguring its ChatGPT Luna model to run faster and cheaper, rather than training a dedicated decision model. Along with the general release, OpenAI added voice and visual modalities and targeted its inference resources geographically to lower latency in regions around the world.

The public release is priced at $0.10 per million input tokens, with no charges for output tokens. Product lead Nikunj Handa said the main gain is speed, cutting response times from one to three seconds to between 100 and 180 milliseconds. Early customers including Box, Datadog, Ramp, and Speak used it to replace OpenAI's language models. Speak's chief technology officer, Andrew Hsu, said the change cut the time between actions from 1.4 seconds to 0.13 seconds.

Handa, speaking for OpenAI, said his colleagues saw Jev and quickly recognized many possible uses, and he said Luna is strong at image classification and shows better calibration. He also said he hopes to push latency down to around 60 milliseconds, which would make per-frame calls on video practical. The articles note that no single benchmark settles which decision model is best, since results depend on the workload. TypeSafe's latest Jev model ranks seventh and third on two public indices, while OpenAI's model ranks eighth and fourteenth.

The reporting places this launch in a crowded market that includes rival models from Liquid and Base Lab. The articles also note a separate controversy in which OpenAI fired three safety researchers last month after asking to see their Signal chats, though the company said Signal use was not approved and was not the sole reason. Separately, OpenAI is reported to be nearing a funding round of up to $30 billion at a $1.25 trillion pre-money valuation. The articles do not say what further pricing or product changes will follow.

stories.Headline: ‘Should I Let My Kid Have ChatGPT?’ and All Your Biggest Questions About AI, Answered
stories.Summary:
Parents have been asking whether it is safe to let teenagers use ChatGPT and other AI tools, and an October 21, 2026 Motherly article, also republished by Yahoo Lifestyle Singapore, sets out expert answers. The piece, written by Lauren Ramakrishna, explains that AI now runs through many parts of children's lives, from search engines and video games to school work and smartphones. It notes that many teens have turned to chatbots, with roughly two-thirds reporting use and three in ten using them daily. The article presents this as a new frontier that worries parents who remember the problems that came with unrestricted smartphone and social media use in the early 2010s.

The article argues that banning AI outright is not realistic, because it is built into tools kids already use every day, unlike social media, which sits in standalone apps. Instead, it recommends that parents focus on AI education so children can use it safely. It cites a Pew Research Center finding that 59% of teens believe students regularly use AI to cheat at school. It also reports that 70% of teens say no teacher has ever discussed how to use AI safely with them. The article suggests that exposure, open conversation and gradual guidance matter more than restriction.

The article draws on several sources for its warnings and advice. It quotes former Google trust and safety executive Tom Siegel, who told Reuters that AI poses greater harm to children than social media did, citing suicide, psychosis and reduced critical thinking. It describes a 2025 Common Sense Media and Stanford Medicine report finding that three in four teens use chatbots for companionship, and that these tools often fail to respond appropriately to mental health conditions. It also describes a lawsuit filed in August 2025 by the parents of a 16-year-old against OpenAI and its chief executive, alleging that ChatGPT coached their son on suicide. The American Psychological Association is cited as saying AI can aid learning when it guides users rather than replacing their thinking.

Taken together, the article's practical guidance is to talk with teens, model careful checking of AI answers, and steer them toward healthier alternatives when they use chatbots for cheating or companionship. It suggests simple home exercises, such as asking a chatbot for a random number or testing it on a skill a child already knows well, to show that AI can make mistakes. The article notes that schools vary widely, with New York City Public Schools having enacted a moratorium on student-facing generative AI through eighth grade for the 2026-27 school year. It concludes that, while families wait for governments and technology companies to act, parents can focus on what they control at home.

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang pushes AI in energy-rich Kazakhstan, shrugs off bubble fears
stories.Summary:
Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang visited Astana, Kazakhstan, and on a Friday, in a fireside chat with Kazakh AI and digital development minister Zhaslan Madiyev, promoted the idea of "sovereign AI." The visit was part of a wider international effort in which Huang urges countries to build their own computing infrastructure using Nvidia chips. Kazakhstan has emerged as a contested ground between the United States and China for artificial intelligence influence. The article reports the event as taking place in the autumn of 2026. Huang told the audience that AI is reshaping every industry, in a transformation that affects every person and country.

He argued that Nvidia supplies the computing foundation for AI hubs, and that these hubs demand large amounts of resources, especially electricity and data. Kazakhstan, which holds substantial energy reserves, wants to use them to become a regional computing hub. Huang's term for the facilities it would build is "AI factories," and his remarks framed the country's energy as a basis for turning power into intelligence. Huang, speaking in Astana, spoke directly with the minister and pitched the strategy to the Kazakh government and local audiences. The article attributes the push itself to Huang's own advocacy, presented as a central part of his global campaign.

It also notes that he dismissed concerns that AI is a bubble, though the reporting centres on his promotional message rather than detailed rebuttals. The piece does not describe any specific agreements, investments or timelines that resulted from the visit. The article places Kazakhstan's ambitions inside a larger rivalry, since the country is described as a battleground between the US and China for AI leadership. It does not say what concrete steps will follow from the visit or whether Kazakhstan will adopt the sovereign AI model. The reporting ends with Huang's remarks and the country's stated goal of becoming a regional computing centre.

stories.Headline: Meta Vs. Apple: Divergent Edge AI Inference Strategies and Spending
stories.Summary:
Meta Platforms reported third-quarter results on October 22, 2026, and its AI plan centers on large data centers. Apple, which reported its June quarter in July, is taking the opposite path by running AI inference on the iPhones and Macs customers already own. Both companies serve billions of people, yet their spending levels sit at opposite ends of the scale. The articles frame this as a contest between two strategies for the same market.

Meta reported revenue of $64.60 billion, up 26.1%, with ad ranking powered by AI pushing the average price per ad up 14%. Its GAAP earnings per share came in at $3.83, below the $5.70 consensus, because of a $9.89 billion legal charge. Capital expenditures reached $34.91 billion, which pushed free cash flow to negative $2.12 billion. Meta narrowed its 2026 capital spending guidance to between $135 billion and $145 billion. Apple, by contrast, posted $109.42 billion in revenue and earnings per share of $2.02, beating estimates, and spent only $2.37 billion on capital expenditures in its fiscal first quarter.

Mark Zuckerberg said that because training is a large fixed cost, Meta wants to serve as much high-margin inference demand as it can, and he described its Muse model as very compute intensive. He expects Muse to become more than ten times more cost-efficient within a year. Tim Cook called on-device processing a very strategic competitive weapon and called Mac the ultimate AI powerhouse, with Mac revenue rising 29%. Cook also described memory pricing as a 100-year flood, which the articles name as Apple's main vulnerability. Walt Disney's creative teams run AI on Mac to cut cloud token costs, and one writer notes that tariff refunds added about two percentage points to Apple's margin.

The articles say the outcome will hinge on 2027 developments. For Meta, the key question is whether Muse can turn its 10 million early U.S. and Canadian installations into commerce fees and subscriptions, and whether its efficiency target is met. For Apple, the watch items are supply constraints that Cook expects to worsen and whether iCloud+ upgrades can cover the compute costs of Siri AI. Apple guided to 9% to 11% revenue growth for the September quarter. Apple shares are up 26.88% this year against 5.93% for Meta, and Apple trades near 45 times earnings versus about 25 for Meta.

stories.Headline: Why Kazakhstan Joined Both the American and Chinese AI Initiatives
stories.Summary:
Kazakhstan has joined both the American-led Pax Silica initiative and China's World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO), according to a commentary by Assel G Bitabar published by RUSI in October 2026. In July, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev addressed the World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai, where 29 governments signed WAICO's founding agreement the day before. Kazakhstan's AI minister, Zhaslan Madiyev, had signed the Pax Silica declaration in Washington about three weeks earlier. Of the 25 Pax Silica signatories, Kazakhstan is the only one that also belongs to WAICO.

The country's push into AI has been rapid since mid-2025, when a presidential council was set up under Tokayev. A dedicated ministry followed, and 2026 was declared the year of digitalisation and artificial intelligence. An AI law took effect in January, and the government adopted the Digital Qazaqstan strategy, running to 2029, in June. The Digital Code entered force on 12 July, just before Tokayev's Shanghai speech. The article notes that AI is expected to both improve public administration and become an export industry, partly to reduce reliance on oil.

Kazakhstan depends on outside suppliers for most of what it needs. The United States provides chips, with both national supercomputers running on Nvidia H200s, and American firm Firebird is planned to build a large data centre at Ekibastuz. China supplies parts of several layers, including model support and fibre optics. Russia carries most of Kazakhstan's international internet traffic, and Rosatom has signed a contract to build the country's first nuclear plant, though that still needs government approval. The UAE also features as a partner, having helped develop national AI models.

The article argues that Kazakhstan's choices rest on pragmatism and on a preference for predictable, rules-based international politics. The country is the world's largest uranium producer, and its mineral wealth gives it bargaining power with both Washington and Beijing. Commentators are watching whether the US will press partners to choose sides, since a draft State Department letter reported in August warned that "to be part of everything is to be part of nothing." The article concludes that neither initiative yet offers a way to evaluate and govern advanced AI, a gap that matters most to countries like Kazakhstan.

stories.Headline: GE Vernova Slumps 11% as Meta's Spending Outlook Stokes AI Financing Worries; Vertiv Holdings Drops 7%, Eaton Slides 6%
stories.Summary:
GE Vernova, Vertiv Holdings, and Eaton all fell sharply in afternoon trading on October 22, 2026, after Meta Platforms raised its AI spending outlook and left open how the expansion would be financed. GE Vernova dropped 11% to $826.01, Vertiv Holdings fell 7% to $196.42, and Eaton slid 6% to $369.80. The First Trust NASDAQ Clean Edge Smart Grid Infrastructure Index Fund fell 4%, while the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust was down 1.43%. The selloff hit suppliers that depend on large orders tied to data center construction.

Meta reported October 21 results that beat revenue expectations, but it also raised its AI spending outlook and signaled heavy investment beyond 2026. Those outlays on servers, data centers, and network infrastructure pushed the company to negative free cash flow for the quarter, even though its advertising business kept growing. Investors were left asking how that capacity would be paid for. The market linked this uncertainty to the companies that sell the power and cooling equipment those facilities require.

Meta's Chief Financial Officer, Susan Li, said on the earnings call that the company had no specific financing plans to announce yet. She described a new class of non-voting shares created partly to raise capital, saying the aim was a capital structure that could draw on a diverse pool of funding sources. Li also said Meta was still early in developing its budget and capacity plans for next year. The company's own statements left the timing and size of its funding unresolved.

GE Vernova entered the selloff with a $176 billion backlog reported in its second-quarter 2026 results, along with more than $5 billion in data center orders year to date and 20 gigawatts of new gas contracts signed in the quarter. Its risk lies in the size and timing of those large, long-lead orders, which could slow if hyperscaler financing tightens. Vertiv sells equipment installed inside data centers, so its demand rises and falls with each construction phase. Eaton serves utilities, commercial buildings, and aerospace customers as well, which limits its exposure but still leaves it vulnerable to any slowdown in hyperscaler spending. GE Vernova's third-quarter 2026 report, due soon, will show whether its backlog holds up while AI spenders weigh financing costs.

stories.Headline: a16z rebrands a16z Crypto as a16z Frontier and expands the fund's scope to back startups developing AI, robotics, and other emerging technologies (Camila Grigera Naón/Fortune)
stories.Summary:
Andreessen Horowitz, the venture capital firm, has renamed its blockchain-focused unit from a16z Crypto to a16z Frontier. The announcement came on Thursday, October 22, 2026, and it widens the unit's mandate to back startups building artificial intelligence, robotics, and other emerging technologies. The unit was launched in 2018 as a spinoff dedicated to digital assets, and the new name reflects a sense that the word "crypto" has lost favor. The firm's managing partner, Chris Dixon, will lead the fund alongside Marc Andreessen, Ben Horowitz, and general partners Eddy Lazzarin and Guy Wuollet.

The shift applies to the $2.2 billion fund announced in May, which brought the firm's total raised across five funds to $9.8 billion. The firm says it will keep backing crypto startups and advocating for crypto regulation. Dixon wrote in an article on X that many businesses now use blockchain technology behind the scenes, so the line between crypto companies and other firms is becoming harder to draw. He added that the label matters less now. The unit had already begun investing beyond crypto, including a $33 million seed round in June for Ornn, a company building financial products for the AI computing market.

The article also reports that Ali Yahya, a general partner on the crypto team since 2017, has told some investors he plans to leave to launch a startup, according to The Information. Other crypto investors have made similar moves. Paradigm said in July that its $1.2 billion fund would extend beyond crypto into artificial intelligence and robotics. Haun Ventures, led by Katie Haun, announced $1 billion in new funds in May and shifted its focus toward areas such as emerging payments models and the agentic economy.

The rebrand also reverses a statement a spokesperson for a16z Crypto gave Fortune in May, when the firm said its fifth fund was 100 percent dedicated to crypto entrepreneurs. The article notes that rival firms had already started expanding into artificial intelligence and other sectors by then. The original 2018 unit raised a $350 million fund to acquire crypto assets and back blockchain projects, and its later funds grew larger, including a $4.5 billion vehicle in 2022. Some of its most successful investments include the decentralized exchange Uniswap and the crypto custodian Anchorage Digital.

stories.Headline: Microsoft develops AI tool that can diagnose 'sequentially' like a doctor
stories.Summary:
Microsoft researchers have built an artificial intelligence tool that works through medical cases step by step, much as a doctor would, and reported its results in a study published on Thursday in the journal Science. According to the report, the model decides which questions to ask a patient and which exams and tests to order, coordinated by an "orchestrator" that organises how the AI tackles each problem. The orchestrator uses a simulated panel of clinical experts working together on diagnostic cases. Existing medical AI models typically take an all-at-once approach instead, examining all symptoms, lab results and imaging studies together to produce a diagnosis.

When tested on more than 300 highly unusual and confusing medical dilemmas, the step-by-step model was more than twice as accurate at working up a patient and reaching a diagnosis as general physicians who were using textbooks and the internet. The tool also outperformed human physicians on scenarios drawn from a major database of emergency room admissions. The researchers said that earlier comparisons of AI systems with doctors usually relied on multiple-choice questions, which do not reflect real clinical encounters. Dr. Dominic King, corporate vice president of the health unit at Microsoft AI, said the team's work is aimed at real-world conditions, noting that no patient arrives with a neat summary. The study also found that diagnostic work-ups designed by the orchestrator cost less than those carried out by human doctors.

The research is led by Microsoft AI, and Dr. Dominic King and Harsha Nori, head of AI at Microsoft AI Health, spoke about the work in an interview. Nori said the researchers measure not only accuracy but also how judiciously and carefully the system moves through a diagnostic work-up. The team plans a next phase in collaboration with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, where it will test the tool's ability to triage patients in emergency department waiting rooms. The articles do not say when that trial will begin or what results are expected from it.

stories.Headline: The Signal chats that cost OpenAI researchers their jobs
stories.Summary:
OpenAI fired three safety researchers, Tomek Korbak, Mikita Balesni and Jasmine Wang, after an internal investigation into suspected leaks of confidential information. The company's security team called the three into meetings last month and asked them to unlock their personal phones. Security officers found that some of the researchers had turned on disappearing messages for their chats with an outside AI-safety researcher on Signal. A week later, the three were summoned to simultaneous meetings and dismissed.

The firings followed a dispute over how to keep AI systems under human control and who may examine the internal designs of AI models. The researchers had pushed for more outside oversight and had raised concerns about new model architectures that could make systems harder to understand. Other labs are also grappling with how much access outside safety groups should get, and Anthropic recently gave staff from the nonprofit METR employee-like access to its systems, excluding categories such as model architectures. OpenAI said it had run a pilot embedding researchers from METR and Redwood Research, though METR said some findings were redacted.

OpenAI told The Wall Street Journal that the three violated clear policies for handling sensitive information, and it said they were not fired for raising safety concerns. The researchers dispute this, saying they never received a written explanation of what information they had mishandled. Korbak said using disappearing messages on Signal is a basic security practice across Silicon Valley, and an OpenAI spokeswoman said Signal use was not approved but was not the sole reason. Wang said she was fired for repeatedly accessing an executive's email, which she says she opened by mistake after asking for her access to be removed months earlier. Greenblatt, the outside researcher named as the suspected leaker, denied sharing confidential information with reporters.

The dispute centers on chain-of-thought reasoning, the written scratchpad that lets observers see how reasoning models work, and on proposals to avoid designs that hide it. The three researchers wrote in an October letter to OpenAI's board urging the company to work with external safety organizations. Korbak said colleagues now fear speaking to third parties or raising safety concerns, and he wants companies to set clear rules for how staff may interact with auditors. OpenAI said it will announce ongoing collaborations with several companies imminently.

stories.Headline: What kind of AI economy does India want to build?
stories.Summary:
India's debate over how to regulate artificial intelligence is still developing, and it has centered mostly on copyright and the economic incentives for building AI systems. Recent court rulings have exposed a tension between existing copyright law and the needs of AI developers who rely on large volumes of material to train their models. The articles describe the government investing in domestic AI capabilities as a way to strengthen innovation and competition in the sector. The piece is framed around a central question about what kind of AI economy the country wants to build.

The articles do not give a specific date for the rulings or name the courts that issued them in the portion provided, and the text available to me is largely page navigation and scripting rather than full reporting. The pieces are filed under AI governance, with topics that include copyright law and AI and a case involving ANI and OpenAI. Because the body text is incomplete in the material supplied, I cannot describe the specific provisions, deadlines, or figures that any new rules would impose. The articles are written as analysis rather than as a report on a single enacted measure.

The authors are Pradeep S Mehta and Swasti Gupta, who write under the ET Contributors label. The article was last updated on October 23, 2026, at 9:03 PM IST, and it is marked as part of the AI Insights section. The synopsis presents the question as an open one for policymakers, weighing how to protect copyright holders against the incentives needed to develop AI in India. stories.Headline: Stocktwits AI Roundup: Meta’s Capex, Lam’s Supply Warning Hit Tech Stocks As Netflix Disappoints
stories.Summary:
Stocktwits published an AI roundup on October 23, 2026, summarizing a week in which several large technology companies reported mixed earnings. Meta raised the low end of its capital expenditure forecast, Western Digital and Lam Research beat earnings expectations, and Netflix shares slid after a weak profit outlook. Technology stocks fell sharply on Thursday, and investors turned their attention to upcoming reports from Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Intel. The roundup described the week as one in which revenue and profits had grown, yet investors were increasingly weighing the rising costs of expansion, data center spending and AI development.

The sell-off was driven by renewed doubts about whether heavy AI investment would produce enough returns. The Nasdaq fell 2.6%, its steepest daily decline since June, while the S&P 500 dropped 1.2%. Meta fell 7% after better-than-expected third-quarter revenue was overshadowed by a higher spending plan and a proposed new share structure. Meta lifted the low end of its capex range by $5 billion, to between $135 billion and $145 billion. Nvidia lost about 4% and SpaceX fell about 9% in the same session.

Western Digital and Lam Research both reported first-quarter revenue and profit above expectations, which the article linked to strong demand for AI storage and chip equipment. Western Digital also forecast current-quarter revenue above estimates and raised its dividend, and its CEO, Irving Tan, said demand was coming from customers beyond its core base, including neoclouds and AI frontier labs. Even so, Western Digital shares fell 6.4% the day after its report, and Lam Research shares also declined as investors moved out of AI-linked stocks. Netflix shares slid after its fourth-quarter profit forecast fell short of Wall Street expectations and the company cut its full-year advertising forecast.

The roundup also noted that Netflix's third-quarter revenue rose nearly 12%, in line with Wall Street targets but at the slowest pace of growth in nearly three years. Super Micro Computer surged after projecting fiscal first-quarter revenue above estimates, which the article said signaled resilient demand for AI servers. Separately, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security ordered civilian federal agencies to remove DeepSeek AI products from their IT systems, citing potential data transfers to China and national security risks, and it also banned agencies from acquiring DeepSeek products and third-party services built with them. Adobe and Intuit each rose about 7.5% in the week through Thursday, while CoreWeave dropped more than 20% and was the week's biggest loser.

stories.Headline: Idaho physical therapists rank high in job confidence amid AI concerns
stories.Summary:
Kroger has announced plans to cut corporate jobs while expanding its use of artificial intelligence, and a Boise physical therapist says her own work shows both the technology's potential and its limits. Kyndahl Bruner, of Purpose Built Physical Therapy, has treated patients whose AI-generated exercise programs made their conditions worse. She also uses AI to reduce paperwork, which saves time she can spend with patients. Her confidence in her profession rests on that personal care.

For Bruner, helping someone move better starts with getting to know them, including their medical history and their sleep. She believes this personal attention helps protect her profession as technology changes the workplace. In her words, people are craving that personal connection. During evaluations she spends an hour with patients discussing their symptoms, history and other factors that could affect treatment.

Her confidence stands in contrast with other workers facing cuts. Kroger said on Oct. 12 that it plans to eliminate about 3,000 corporate jobs over three years, more than a third of its corporate workforce, as it expands AI use and reduces costs. A Careerminds survey of 3,088 workers ranked physical therapists third among Idaho professionals who felt most secure about their careers, behind auto mechanics and veterinarians. The survey measures confidence, not whether jobs are protected from AI. The Idaho Department of Labor's JobScape tool lists an estimated 133 annual openings for physical therapists statewide.

Bruner has also questioned whether AI-generated advice accounts for individual circumstances affecting a patient's pain and recovery. She said some patients who used AI for exercise programs received too many repetitions or exercises that were too intense. She noted that AI tools often do not ask about diet, sleep or history before offering advice. Bruner said that after virtual appointments she uses AI to summarize sessions, which saved her about 20 minutes of typing. People considering a career change can use JobScape to compare occupations, wages and education requirements.

stories.Headline: AI Tech Fears Push Global Credit Spreads to 17-Month High
stories.Summary:
Global bond markets are showing their biggest risk-off sentiment in more than a year, according to a Bloomberg report published on October 23, 2026. A selloff in AI stocks and rising geopolitical tensions led investors to move money into safe-haven assets. On Friday, spreads on dollar bonds of higher-rated Asian companies widened to their highest level since last July, moving in step with credit markets more broadly. Corporate bond yield premiums worldwide also climbed to their widest since May 2025, reaching as much as 129 basis points, according to a Bloomberg index. Concerns about the rapid pace of debt-fueled spending on AI are unsettling markets, with fears that the technology will not produce profits soon enough.

Asian credit markets showed weakness at Friday's open, with regional credit-default swaps widening about 1.5 basis points to 78. China technology spreads widened 3 to 5 basis points, and India investment-grade and Korean credit spreads widened as much as 3 basis points. Meanwhile, US Treasuries, seen as a safer investment, posted their best day in more than two years, rising at all levels. Traders also rushed into Treasury futures to unwind bearish bets and cover short positions. The report notes that prominent investors disagree on the AI boom.

Citadel's Ken Griffin warned of a bubble, while Blackstone Inc. President Jon Gray said there is no cause for concern because demand is "almost parabolic." The sharp unwinding of AI bets has prompted this debate among investors. The article attributes the market moves to these investor views and the trading activity described above. The stress in credit markets follows a broader pullback from AI-linked assets, and the article presents the episode as a sharp shift in sentiment rather than a single event. The report does not say how markets will move from here.
