stories.Headline: Turning Database Grading into RL Rewards: Post-Training Agents with ThinkingBox
stories.Summary:
Microsoft and Hugging Face published a follow-up on October 22, 2026, describing how they turned ThinkingBox, a benchmark that checks an agent's work against the final database state, into a reinforcement learning reward. ThinkingBox-Training is now available on GitHub. The team built a training pool from tasks outside the 507-task ThinkingBox-Bench, selected to be neither already solved nor hopeless for the base model, and fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B with GRPO for 50 steps. Average success on the benchmark rose from 51.70% to 60.78%, and tasks passed on all twenty attempts rose from 38 to 107. The approach uses the executable check on terminal database state as the reward signal, rather than grading tool calls.

The team estimated each task's success probability once using the base policy and kept that training pool fixed throughout the run, a method they call offline policy-relative difficulty. The fine-tuned checkpoint was evaluated at step 50 on the benchmark it had never trained on. Gains appeared in all five domains on pass@1 and observed 20/20, while pass@20 fell in three of five domains. The authors, a joint Microsoft and Hugging Face team including Mirco Milletari, Xiang Jiang, Sergio Paniego and Zhuochun Li, said the results show repeatability improved while at-least-once coverage slightly declined.

They describe this pattern as consistent with sharpening, where probability shifted toward trajectories that work reliably. The write-up also gives a cost comparison in which the fine-tuned model's estimated cost per dependable task fell from about $8.00 to a figure they place near several frontier models, though they note these are comparative serving estimates rather than actual bills. The post does not say what the team plans next. It presents the results as a follow-up to the first ThinkingBox post and points readers to the GitHub repository for the training stack.

Articles.Title: Turning Database Grading into RL Rewards: Post-Training Agents with ThinkingBox

stories.Headline: Liquid AI Launches RIPL, a Real-Time Inference Engine for Sub-50 ms LFMs
stories.Summary:
Liquid AI has announced RIPL, short for Real-time Inference Pipeline, a low-latency engine that serves its Liquid Foundation Models inside live request paths. The company says RIPL returns complete generated responses end to end in under 50 milliseconds and that this latency holds while traffic arrives continuously at peak load. The announcement was published on MarkTechPost on October 22, 2026. The article is based on Liquid AI's own announcement and benchmark figures, so the performance numbers are self-reported.

RIPL is aimed at enterprise deployments on NVIDIA H100, H200, B200 and RTX PRO 6000 GPUs, and the benchmarks were run on a single B200. Liquid AI compared its LFM2.5 models on RIPL against Qwen3.5 models on the open-source vLLM engine, reporting p95 latency gains of 5.6 to 28.4 times. The strongest result was LFM2.5-1.2B at 155.8 milliseconds p95 versus 4,431 milliseconds for Qwen3.5-0.8B on 256-token inputs with 128-token outputs, a 28.4 times gap at 400 requests per second. The weakest result was LFM2.5-2.6B on the same longer requests, at 449.1 milliseconds versus 2,499 milliseconds, a 5.6 times gap, meaning the sub-50 millisecond target was not met for that workload. Shorter 32-token requests did reach tens of milliseconds, with LFM2.5-1.2B at 34.6 milliseconds p95 at 1,000 requests per second.

The article says most serving stacks are tuned for large batches and long agentic jobs, where a few seconds per request is acceptable. Latency-sensitive uses such as search ranking, fraud checks and payment authorization need answers in milliseconds. Liquid AI argues that teams often fall back to classical models for these paths because LLM serving is too slow, and RIPL is meant to remove that trade-off. The company says it optimizes the full path from request arrival to completed response, and it attributes part of the gain to the engine itself rather than the model architecture alone.

Liquid AI named Shopify as a customer deploying LFMs across latency-sensitive commerce workloads. The article describes example workloads with latency budgets, including payment risk scoring at 50 milliseconds, search reranking at 30 milliseconds and credit decisioning at 150 milliseconds. Liquid AI presents these as targets its models can serve, and the article gives no independent verification of them. Further details on pricing, availability and third-party testing are not covered in the article.

Articles.Title: Liquid AI Launches RIPL, a Real-Time Inference Engine for Sub-50 ms LFMs

stories.Headline: Gradium Open-Sources Phonon, a 31M-Parameter On-Device TTS Model Under Apache 2.0
stories.Summary:
Gradium, a Paris-based voice AI company spun out of Kyutai, has open-sourced Phonon, a family of small text-to-speech models designed to run directly on devices. The English Phonon 31M model has 31 million parameters, excluding the audio tokenizer, and ships under the Apache 2.0 license in a 64.5 MB file. A 40M size is also available at 74.6 MB. Gradium says the models generate natural speech locally, without a cloud call, a GPU or a per-character fee.

The models run on CPUs, phones, a Raspberry Pi 5, browsers using WebAssembly or WebGPU, and NVIDIA GPUs. The article reports that Phonon 31M produces its first audio in about 7 milliseconds on a CPU and outputs 24 kHz mono audio. The 31M English model supports 37 built-in voices, while the 40M English model uses CC BY-NC 4.0 and multilingual versions cover English, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese, with the multilingual model offering 102 voices. In Gradium's tests, its English models scored above the other open models it compared, with Phonon 40M at 2117 Elo and Phonon 31M at 2098, compared with 2043 for Kokoro. On a 500-sentence hard set full of numbers, emails and postal codes, Phonon 31M had a 1.70% word error rate against 3.50% for Kokoro, though on an easier public set Kokoro edged it out, 0.45% to 0.51%.

Gradium published these results and the model weights itself, and the article attributes the benchmark figures to Gradium's own evaluations. The model uses a causal transformer backbone with a SentencePiece tokenizer that reads raw text without phoneme conversion, and it was distilled from a larger teacher model trained on an NVIDIA H100 cluster. The work builds on research from Kyutai and its Pocket TTS project. The articles do not say what comes next for the project or whether further releases are planned.

Articles.Title: Gradium Open-Sources Phonon, a 31M-Parameter On-Device TTS Model Under Apache 2.0

stories.Headline: Cohere Releases Rerank 5 With Passage-Level Context Focus and Calibrated Scores
stories.Summary:
Cohere AI has released Rerank 5, a new family of search reranking models offered in two tiers, Pro and Fast. The company announced the release in an October 22, 2026 article on MarkTechPost. Rerank 5 sits between a search system and a large language model, reordering retrieved results before they reach the model. It adds two developer features, Context Focus and calibrated relevance scores, which Cohere presents as a way to send fewer and better tokens to the model.

Both tiers support a 32K token context window and more than 100 languages, and they can also rerank semi-structured data such as JSON, tables and YAML. Developers can run the models through Cohere's hosted API, Model Vault, Microsoft Foundry, Amazon SageMaker, or a private virtual cloud or on-premises setup. Cohere benchmarks speed on a single NVIDIA A100 chip. The parameter count has not been disclosed, and no open weights or quantized versions were mentioned. Upgrading requires no re-indexing, because developers only change the model name and keep their existing keyword, vector or hybrid search.

Cohere reports its own results, and the article states that Pro ranks first on 39 of 46 composite datasets in the company's evaluation. Pro scores 82.2 on the BRIGHT benchmark, 5.8 points above Voyage AI Rerank 3, but its median latency is 11.7 seconds per 96-document request, compared with 4.1 seconds for Fast. Context Focus is off by default and returns scored character spans with start and end positions. In one test across 30 question-answering datasets, removing half the retrieved text kept 96% of answer quality, and removing three quarters kept 87%. Cohere's own search-agent tests show that the full stack used 35% fewer tokens than BM25 alone while raising accuracy.

The calibrated scores are designed so that a score of 0.7 corresponds to roughly a 70% chance a document is useful. Cohere measured expected calibration error against human graders and NIST assessors, reporting about 0.06 for Rerank 5 compared with 0.234 and 0.307 for Voyage AI Rerank 3. Developers could therefore filter by threshold instead of a fixed number of results, and an agent could detect when nothing relevant was returned. Cohere says the figures are self-reported and that it ran the competitor models itself. The article gives no date for general availability beyond the release announcement, and it does not say what independent evaluators have found.

Articles.Title: Cohere Releases Rerank 5 With Passage-Level Context Focus and Calibrated Scores

stories.Headline: 4 AI Agents Trained by Google in Minecraft: 605 Deaths Later, They Independently Wrote Code to Defeat the Ender Dragon Boss Head-On
stories.Summary:
Four AI agents built by Google DeepMind, running on its Gemini 4 Argon model, were placed in a randomly generated Minecraft survival world and given one goal: defeat the Ender Dragon. According to the article, the team took 27 hours and 14 minutes and wrote 2,783 segments of code on its own, dying 605 times along the way. No strategy guide, pre-assigned roles, or human-written completion program was supplied. The findings were described in a paper published on October 15, 2026, titled "A team of Gemini 4 Argon agents beats Minecraft."

The setup used Minecraft Java Edition 1.20.4 in Survival mode on Easy difficulty, with no cheat commands. Each agent controlled one character, read the game state through the open-source tool Mineflayer, and wrote JavaScript to direct its actions. Roughly ten minutes in, one agent proposed dividing labor in the chat channel, and the four settled into roles: one handled resource logistics, one tool making and exploration, one key technical breakthroughs, and one resource exploration and the final battle. The article notes these roles were not fixed in advance and shifted as the game progressed. Less than two hours in, the team had iron tools and diamonds and had built a portal to the Nether.

Deaths were treated as lessons rather than total failures. The article gives one example: when one agent died carrying 12 blaze powders, which were destroyed by a Ghast fireball, teammates warned of transport dangers and the cause was logged in shared memory for reuse. The article also reports about 24,000 model calls, roughly 1.35 billion input tokens and 16 million output tokens, with 91% of input tokens drawn from context cache. Each agent spent about 40% of its time generating game programs and the rest analyzing results and reasoning. The researchers gave each agent persistent memory and a shared team memory to handle context growth.

The article places the work against earlier efforts: the 2023 Voyager research using GPT-4, and the AltoClef project, which cleared Minecraft in May 2021 but relied on developer-written task logic. It also cites a June 2026 PUBG Ally test by KRAFTON and NVIDIA. The article cautions that results are not yet stable, with about 22% of game programs erroring and the server restarted six times. It estimates the run cost around 520 US dollars at discounted API prices, and says the paper has not yet shown repeated clears on random maps. The article closes by noting that, for now, humans still hold the controllers.

Articles.Title: 4 AI Agents Trained by Google in Minecraft: 605 Deaths Later, They Independently Wrote Code to Defeat the Ender Dragon Boss Head-On - 36Kr

stories.Headline: Altman Exclusive Interview 2025: Why Prioritizing People Is Non-Negotiable in the AI Era
stories.Summary:
Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, gave a wide-ranging interview covering AI-driven scientific discovery, personal AI assistants, computing demand, model personality, consciousness and the company's hardware plans. He argued that AI is moving from a tool toward something that can help discover new knowledge, but that the future must remain people-oriented. He said recursive self-improvement could happen and is extremely dangerous to push forward. He also said today's models have no consciousness and that the company should not give them a personality of their own. Altman further said OpenAI needs new consumer hardware because the technology calls for a new form factor.

On discovery, Altman said he expects AI to help in fields such as mathematics, biology, drug development, materials science and new energy, and he said he hopes to find candidate drugs for major diseases within a few years. He noted that FDA approval takes time and that the process may also need reform. He said a major physics discovery is what excites him most right now. On work, he argued that programmers have never been busier or more influential, even though the nature of their work has changed, and that the world's demand for software is far greater than many expected. He also said the people who use AI most are busier than ever and need to make more decisions, which can leave them drained.

On the broader stakes, Altman said the top one percent of users currently drive heavy AI use while most people have not used it the way power users do. He argued that computing demand may keep rising if the cost of high-quality intelligence falls, and he advised getting as many GPUs as possible. He described a personal AI assistant revolution that began with OpenClaw, which he said can monitor what people care about and handle tasks, and he said OpenAI may eventually launch consumer hardware to support it. He cautioned that people often want short-term pleasing responses rather than what helps them over months, and he said important life advice should come from people rather than AI.

Altman's remarks on consciousness were the most open-ended. He said he believes today's models are not conscious, but that no one can be certain, and he said the debate could shape questions about AI rights that society must still answer. He suggested that the consciousness question should not be used to weaken human control over the future. The articles do not say what specific policy or product steps OpenAI will take next on these topics, so the interview's concrete commitments remain limited.

Articles.Title: Altman Exclusive Interview 2025: Why Prioritizing People Is Non-Negotiable in the AI Era - 36Kr

stories.Headline: Anthropic Unveils New AI Governance Architecture – Redefining Capital Rules for Global AI Companies
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the AI company behind the Claude models, has drawn attention for a governance design that departs from the usual Silicon Valley model ahead of a possible public listing, reported in an article dated October 22, 2026. Rather than using dual-class share structures that keep voting power with founders, the company combines a Public Benefit Corporation, a legal form that lets directors weigh public safety and social impact alongside shareholder returns, with a long-term independent trust. The trust holds no shares and shares in no profits, yet it holds the real control. Former Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke is named among the trustees. The article notes that this structure challenges the capital market's long-held expectation that listed companies prioritize shareholder returns.

The trustees hold two core powers, according to the article. They may replace most members of the board of directors, and the company must report major transactions to the trust five days in advance. Those transactions include large-scale unconventional debt, the sale of more than half of the equity, and the transfer of core AI models that reach a defined threshold. Commercial law scholars cited in the article read the five-day requirement as more than a simple notice, since it could work as a soft veto once the trust suspects a safety risk. The article describes this as essentially different from the AB share model, because the power sits with a third party outside the shareholders and founding team.

Anthropic's design, in effect, gives up part of shareholders' ordinary rights in advance. The article describes the company's structure as a choice made by its leadership, which chose to pair a PBC with an independent trust. It presents Dario Amodei, a co-founder who previously served as Vice President of Research at OpenAI, as the company's founder behind the Claude models. The article says the company's leadership judged that a PBC alone cannot protect against shareholders or founders pushing for commercial gain, which is why the trust was added. It does not provide direct quotations from company officials on this point, so the reasoning is reported through the article's own analysis.

The article places Anthropic between two rivals. OpenAI uses a non-profit foundation at the top to hold control over a profit-making subsidiary, while Elon Musk's xAI briefly registered as a PBC before switching back to an ordinary commercial company. Analysts in the article see the market's reaction as split: primary-market investors may value the safety-focused narrative and regulatory protection, while secondary-market investors may discount the shares because shareholders cannot influence decisions the trustees could block. The article suggests the listing will likely proceed smoothly amid strong AI demand, but that disputes over trustee power may recur after the shares begin trading. It also notes that the company's experience will serve as a reference for other large model companies preparing to go public.

Articles.Title: Anthropic Unveils New AI Governance Architecture – Redefining Capital Rules for Global AI Companies - eu.36kr.com

stories.Headline: IMF highlights AI-driven growth potential in Middle East, Central Asia - Xinhua
stories.Summary:
The International Monetary Fund said on Thursday, October 22, 2026, that artificial intelligence adoption could raise annual economic growth in the Middle East and Central Asia by 0.1 to 0.6 percentage points over the medium term. The estimate depends on how digitally ready each country is and how well it can bring the technology into productive activity. The assessment was presented at a joint press conference in Dubai held by the Dubai International Financial Center and the fund, drawing on its October Regional Economic Outlook for the two regions. The fund's findings were reported by Xinhua from Dubai.

The report argues that AI offers the region a chance to lift productivity and strengthen growth over the coming years. It points to several Gulf Cooperation Council countries, including the United Arab Emirates, which are making large investments meant to establish them as global AI hubs. The IMF raised its 2027 growth forecast for the UAE to 7.7 percent, a rise of 2.4 percentage points from its April projection. It estimated that AI investment alone would add about 0.5 percentage points to the UAE's annual growth.

The fund stressed that sustained spending on digital infrastructure, education, skills development and innovation is needed to raise productivity and support economic diversification. In its policy guidance, the IMF said it had provided about 48 billion U.S. dollars in financing to countries in the Middle East and Central Asia since 2020. It also said it carried out 437 technical assistance and capacity development projects across 31 countries during fiscal year 2026. The articles do not describe any further steps or deadlines beyond these findings.

Articles.Title: IMF highlights AI-driven growth potential in Middle East, Central Asia - Xinhua

stories.Headline: Asymptote Labs Lands $5.5 Million Seed for AI Agent Runtime Security
stories.Summary:
Asymptote Labs has raised $5.5 million in seed funding to build runtime control and visibility infrastructure for enterprise AI agents, according to a SecurityWeek report published October 21, 2026. Tower Research Ventures led the round, which was oversubscribed, with Lytical Ventures, 1984 Ventures, and South Park Commons also taking part. The company plans to use the capital for product development, engineering expansion, and go-to-market work. The round is aimed at a gap the company's founders see in how security teams monitor autonomous tools that reach sensitive corporate data. The company's foundation is Beacon, an open source telemetry layer that standardizes activity from more than 20 agent harnesses, including Cursor, Codex, and Claude Code.

Beacon normalizes that activity into a unified data model that extends the OpenTelemetry framework. A commercial enterprise platform sits on top of this open source core and intercepts live agent activity to enforce policy guardrails at both the prompt and tool execution levels. According to the article, this lets the system steer agents away from unsafe behavior and block risky actions before they happen. Chief executive Justin D'Souza and chief technology officer Shukan Shah founded the company, and both previously built defenses at Doppel. D'Souza said AI agents are becoming a new operating layer inside companies while the infrastructure to understand and control them has not kept pace.

He said the team saw the problem firsthand while building agents at Doppel. He also argued that as companies deploy thousands of agents, their runtime data will become one of the most valuable assets they own. The article places the funding within a broader push by security startups into AI and autonomous system defense, though it does not detail the company's customers or timeline for commercial release. It does not say how many companies are currently using the platform or what pricing will look like. The report does not indicate further funding plans or specific milestones beyond the stated uses of the seed capital.

Articles.Title: Asymptote Labs Lands $5.5 Million Seed for AI Agent Runtime Security - SecurityWeek

stories.Headline: Kyndryl: Enterprises must fix security gaps before embracing AI
stories.Summary:
Kevin O'Leary, head of security and resiliency at Kyndryl, told CRN Asia that enterprises should close existing security and governance gaps before layering AI onto their operations, and the interview was published on October 22, 2026. He said many organizations, especially in the region, still have outdated documentation and weak change management, and AI cannot build those foundations on its own. He noted that AI tools read whatever data they are given and can spot gaps, but they cannot create the fixes without human intervention. Governance models, risk and compliance frameworks, and documented processes need to exist before AI is added on top of them.

O'Leary also raised data sovereignty, which he described as a question that has long shaped cloud security and now applies to AI as well. He asked where data moves when an AI model accesses it and whether the model simply reads the data in place or transfers it, calling this partly a philosophical question about data flows. He said some countries are starting to develop their own models to pursue truly sovereign AI. Kyndryl, he added, has deployed more AI and agentic AI into its internal security operations center, with guardrails protecting customer and company data, and it offers that capability to customers as a service.

O'Leary said that every cybersecurity partner now has AI embedded somewhere in its technology, which he described as an expectation rather than a differentiator. He said the real question is where AI is applied in an environment and what output it produces, and he described a feedback loop between Kyndryl and its partners that shapes their roadmaps. He added that partners that fail to keep pace with the market risk losing customers, while those pushing at the edges attract the most attention. He said Kyndryl must determine which partners suit each situation.

Looking ahead, O'Leary warned that pressure on organizations will grow, particularly from frontier models. He recalled warnings of a surge in patching needed after Mythos AI, and said that surge has not yet arrived because companies asked Anthropic not to release it, with a typical 90-day window before vulnerabilities must be disclosed. He said that even this slower trickle is hard for healthcare and finance firms with very small patching windows, many of which carry a long tail of unaddressed low-impact vulnerabilities. He expects more critical patches to go unaddressed, making virtual patching, zero trust, and resilient-by-design approaches more important. He said AI's strength lies less in discovering zero-day flaws than in chaining previously unconnected low-level vulnerabilities into serious exploits, and he concluded that the cybersecurity arms race will keep piling new risks on old ones.

Articles.Title: Kyndryl: Enterprises must fix security gaps before embracing AI - CRN Asia

stories.Headline: carsales unveils new retail channel and some AI tools
stories.Summary:
carsales used its Open House '27 event in Sydney on 22 October 2026 to outline a new automotive retail channel for carmakers and dealer networks. The proposal aims to help manufacturers and dealers reach buyers earlier in the purchase process, taking them through research, comparison and ordering in one place. At the same event, the company also unveiled new AI-assisted shopping tools for consumers and formally launched Iggy, an AI-based intelligence platform for marketers. The moves respond to a crowded market, where carsales says 79 brands compete for buyers and 54 models are on sale that were not available a year earlier. Under the model, consumers could discover vehicles suited to their needs, compare options, configure a car and connect with retailers through a single experience.

carsales says buyers may now take up to six months to decide, and that 60 per cent of car intenders on its platform are already considering a new vehicle. The company argues this gives carmakers and dealers a chance to align more closely with shoppers already active on the site. Buyers could choose how far to take the process on carsales, from researching and enquiring to booking a test drive or placing an order. The strategy reflects a broader push by automotive marketplaces to move beyond listings and advertising into transaction and retail activity.

Ollie Nugent, Head of Consumer Product at carsales, described the concept as a more connected journey for buyers and sellers. He said the company sees a chance to bring the new car journey together, from research through to placing an order. Nugent said dealers could gain access to more informed, purchase-ready buyers, while manufacturers could gain a new retail channel closer to consumers. Nicholas Bailly, General Manager, Advertising at carsales, said that more brands are competing for Australian buyers than ever and that consumers are less loyal than the company has measured before.

He said the goal is to help automotive brands influence decisions in the place people already trust to find their next car. Iggy sits within Ignition, carsales' self-serve advertising and campaign management platform, and is designed for marketers who can ask business questions in plain language. It brings together AI agents covering audiences, inventory, competitors, campaigns, measurement and creative insights. According to carsales, the system draws on more than 16 million logged-in members, 3 billion automotive shopping signals each quarter, VIN-level inventory data and transaction signals.

Stephen Kyefulumya, General Manager, Media Product & Technology at carsales, said the industry's problem is less a lack of data than a failure to connect it to purchase outcomes. The announcements build on the company's One Platform. Every Advantage. strategy, which seeks to link consumer experiences, retail and marketing intelligence within one ecosystem.

Articles.Title: carsales unveils new retail channel and some AI tools - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: AI now helps Australians choose brands, study finds
stories.Summary:
A research report from the Australian Centre for AI in Marketing, published on 22 October 2026, argues that brands must now win the approval of both artificial intelligence systems and consumers. The study, called The Navigators' AI Brandscape 2026, surveyed 1,736 Australians and found that 39 per cent had used generative AI to help choose a brand, product or service. The report says the early stage of the customer journey is becoming harder for marketers to see, because more people use AI tools to research purchases before they buy. As a result, a brand can be ruled out before the customer ever makes a final choice.

The research also shows that consumers are cautious about letting AI take full control. Just 11 per cent of respondents said they would allow AI to make a purchase decision, even for low-stakes products. The report describes a gap between using AI for research and handing it decision-making power, and it urges marketers to understand which tasks people are willing to delegate. ACAM's Customer Delegation Framework asks four questions: whether AI can do the job, whether it is worth using, whether the customer stays in charge, and whether such use is socially normal. Customers are more willing to hand over tasks when AI is clearly useful and convenient, while worries about control, trust and social acceptance hold back wider use.

Louise Cummins, Chief Executive Officer and Co-Founder of ACAM, said that brands now have to be chosen twice, first by a customer's AI and then by the customer. She warned that a brand missing from the AI's shortlist may never get the chance to make its case. Cummins said marketers need to know what information AI uses to make recommendations and what earns customer trust. Duncan Egan, Vice President of Enterprise Marketing for Asia Pacific and Japan at Adobe, which supported the report, said teams should focus on orchestrating connected experiences rather than only creating campaigns. Egan added that people should remain in control of strategy, brand and the customer relationship.

The report sets this shift against a gap in readiness. Its 2026 AI in Marketing Benchmark, conducted with Kantar, found that 83 per cent of participating Australian organisations sat at levels one to three of ACAM's six-level maturity scale, and none reached levels five or six. Separate research from Twilio and YouGov, cited in the report, found that 78 per cent of people had used AI-powered customer service but only 39 per cent were satisfied, and 84 per cent wanted an easy way to reach a person. The publication, the third in ACAM's research programme, includes a 90-day plan for marketing leaders and examples from Budget Direct, ANZ, Telstra and Woolworths.

Articles.Title: AI now helps Australians choose brands, study finds - IT Brief Australia
